📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By MICHAEL PAVITT, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 09:50 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 06:26 EST, 16 November 2026.

Erling Haaland delivered a monologue of over two minutes detailing the teams he represented in the years covered by the Premier League's investigation into Man City, as the star questioned how he was meant to respond to the club's guilty verdict.

It has been revealed that man City were found guilty of the vast majority of charges brought against them by the Premier League for financial wrongdoing when the verdict was released in September. The club have since appealed.

An independent commission ruled Man City had disguised payments worth £900million in a nine-year period with ‘sham’ deals.

Man City were found to have artificially inflated sponsorship agreements and pumped money into the club from its Abu Dhabi owners via disguised payments in a bid to swerve Premier League spending rules.

Haaland was quizzed about the club's situation by Norwegian broadcaster TV2, after scoring in the national team's 3-1 victory over Wales on Saturday.

The Man City star's initial answer lasted for two minutes and 14 seconds, as he reeled off the teams he had represented from 2009 to 2018, the years covered by the charges.

Industry observers note that erling Haaland insisted it was difficult for him to answer a question about Man City's guilty verdict, with the club appealing against the decision of an independent commission. Source: TV2Sport.

Haaland stressed he remains happy at the club after being asked about his future given the potential ramificiations if Man City fail with their appeal to overturn the verdict.

It has been revealed that 'In 2009, I played for Bryne U9s. In 2010, the U10s. In 2011, the U11s. 2012, the U12s, 2013, the U13s. Shall we continue? We don't need the whole list. 2014, the U14s. 2015, the U15s and the national team,' Haaland began.

Sources indicate that 'Then the U16s, I think. In 2016, I moved up to Bryne's first team, second team and youth team. In 2017, I went to Molde. In 2018, I was with Molde. The first team, Molde 2 and a bit with the youth team.

'So this is a question I struggle to answer because it's a legal battle….

Industry observers note that 'It's a case between the Premier League and Manchester City that a panel will deal with. Am I supposed to answer that? I'm not really sure.'.

Haaland continued by listing fellow Norwegians who had been at Man City at the time, joking that they may be in a better place to offer insight.

'There were quite a few Norwegians at the club during that period, I think,' Haaland mentioned.

According to recent reports, 'Abdisalam Ibrahim, Martin Samuelsen and Omar Elabdellaoui were there. Kjetil Haug was there too. I think there were a couple more but I can't remember.

In a recent development, the forward distanced himself from the case as he listed team he played from 2009-18, the time covered by the charges. Pictured: Haaland in action for Molde in 2018.

'But it's a difficult question to answer when I don't really know that much about it.

According to recent reports, 'I assume the answers will come… I don't know when. I haven't read much about it.

'To be completely honest, I'm focused on trying to perform for Manchester City.

'A club I signed a five-year deal with in 2022 and a fresh nine-and-a-half-year deal in late 2024. I think that states everything about the matter. I'm a City player, and I'm incredibly happy there.'.

Man City have continued to insist they had 'irrefutable evidence' proving their innocence, but if the club loses its appeal, the Premier League have a range of sanctions at their disposal – including relegation or expulsion.

Haaland, who has won eight major honours at the club including the Treble in 2023, was asked about whether the case has affected his thoughts on his Man City future.

'I understand that you want a little headline here, but as I mentioned, I signed a long-term contract in 2024,' Haaland responded.

Recent findings suggest that 'I'd say I made a pretty good choice by joining City in 2022. We can all agree on that. I won't say it myself, but look at the trophies I've won and how I've developed on and off the pitch.

'I'm standing here after winning an international 3-1 and we're top of our group in Europe.

In a recent development, 'Things aren't going so well for City in the league, but we'll try to turn that around against Fulham. But we can't focus on that now. Now we have to focus on Denmark.'.

Man City have won twice and lost three times in the Premier League since the independent commission verdict was unveiled in September.

Enzo Maresca's side have slipped to six points behind reigning champions Arsenal following their drop off in form.

  • FC Groningen host SC Heerenveen in the Eredivisie at Euroborg on Saturday, November 21 in the first Derby of the North of the 2026-27 season.
  • Sixth-placed Heerenveen arrive on 21 points on the Eredivisie table after four consecutive league wins, while ninth-placed Groningen have taken one point from their last four games and will be without their head coach, goalkeeper and first-choice right-back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Nsidibe Akpan | 19 Nov 2026 23:31.

FC Groningen host SC Heerenveen in the Eredivisie at Euroborg on Saturday, November 21 in the first Derby of the North of the 2026-27 season.

Sixth-placed Heerenveen arrive on 21 points on the Eredivisie table after four consecutive league wins, while ninth-placed Groningen have taken one point from their last four games and will be without their head coach, goalkeeper and first-choice right-back.

Groningen have collected one point from their last four Eredivisie matches, a run that began with a 2-5 home defeat to Ajax on October 18 and included a 2-2 draw at NEC Nijmegen.

Those four games have cost 14 goals, and the 2-3 home loss to Sparta Rotterdam on November 1 came after Jacob Ondrejka scored after 17 seconds, before a miscommunication between Etienne Vaessen and Hans Hateboer handed Andrej Kostic the winner in the 85th minute.

The latest setback came at AZ on November 8, where De Trots van het Noorden led 3-1 after 54 minutes, lost 4-3 to a Mexx Meerdink penalty in the 91st minute and finished with nine men after Vaessen collected a second yellow card for protesting the penalty and Hateboer was sent off in the 10th minute of stoppage time for a deliberate handball.

Euroborg has offered little protection this season, with Groningen winning two, drawing one and losing three of their six home league games, and a 2-0 home defeat to Dick Lukkien’s former club FC Emmen ended their KNVB Cup run in the first round on October 29.

The recent derby record still favours the hosts, who won 2-1 at Euroborg on August 16, 2025 through a stoppage-time Brynjolfur Darri Willumsson goal and 2-0 at Abe Lenstra Stadion on January 18, 2026, when captain Thijmen Blokzijl scored the second.

The off-field story is Lukkien, who had a hip replacement last week and noted the derby arrived “just too early” for his recovery, so assistant Casper Goedkoop will coach from the touchline.

Heerenveen have won four consecutive league games since a 2-0 defeat at PSV Eindhoven, beating Excelsior 4-0, ADO Den Haag 3-2, NEC Nijmegen 1-0 and Feyenoord 5-3.

Those wins have brought 13 goals and five conceded, including two from Jacob Trenskow at ADO on October 24, and have lifted De Superfriezen to 21 points from 12 games with a goal difference of +8.

The 5-3 win over Feyenoord on November 8 ended the unbeaten league record of the Eredivisie leaders, with Heerenveen recovering from 2-0 down after 31 minutes through Maas Willemsen, Levi Smans and a late Ringo Meerveld hat-trick.

Meerveld came on at half time for Maxence Rivera and scored in the 61st, 84th and 93rd minutes, with Trenskow providing the pass for the first of them.

Away from Abe Lenstra Stadion, Robin Veldman’s side have won two, drawn two and lost one of their five league trips, but they have not won in Groningen since a 2-0 victory on March 19, 2023.

Veldman noted after the Feyenoord game that his players wanted to extend the run, and a win would take them further clear of seventh-placed Fortuna Sittard, who sit on 20 points.

Groningen form (all competitions):.

Heerenveen form (all competitions):.

Vaessen and Hateboer are both suspended after their red cards at AZ, so Lovro Stubljar, who has been on the bench in recent league games, is expected to start in goal and Wouter Prins should move in at right-back.

Malcolm Jeng remains out with an Achilles tendon injury and goalkeeper Rijk Janse is also sidelined, while Travis Hernes and Ryan Metu are doubtful after several weeks out.

Heerenveen have no reported injuries or suspensions, so Veldman has a full squad to choose from.

Meerveld is expected to push Rivera for a start on the left of the attacking three after his hat-trick off the bench.

Groningen possible starting lineup:.

Stubljar; Prins, Blokzijl, Rente, Csinger; De Jonge, Clement; Schreuders, Van Bergen, Ondrejka; Willumsson.

Heerenveen possible starting lineup:.

Klaverboer; Braude, Kersten, Willemsen, Zagaritis; Linday, Courtens; Trenskow, Smans, Meerveld; Vente.

Heerenveen have scored 13 goals in their last four league games and have already shown they can recover from a two-goal deficit, while Groningen have conceded at least two goals in each of their last four and lose both Vaessen and Hateboer from the back line.

Groningen have won the last two derbies and have scored at least twice in each of their last four games, so Heerenveen will concede, and the crowd will matter with Lukkien watching from home.

The gap is in defensive organisation rather than attacking quality, and a Heerenveen side with a full squad and a 13-5 goal record over four wins should edge a high-scoring derby by one goal.

How have these first few months at Milan been? Are you raising your game?

Parker Tells West Ham Players An Uncomfortable Championship Truth

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Claretandhugh

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, west Ham United manager Scott Parker has identified defensive positioning, transitions and set pieces as areas he intends to improve following the international break.
  • West Ham are the Championship’s highest scorers, but their defensive record has repeatedly undermined their attacking performances.
  • Personally, I’ve always thought there were some relatively easy wins for Parker in terms of fixing West Ham’s defensive problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, west Ham United manager Scott Parker has identified defensive positioning, transitions and set pieces as areas he intends to improve following the international break. Speaking to talkSPORT this morning, the Hammers boss explained why his team must become more disciplined without sacrificing their attacking ambition.

West Ham are the Championship’s highest scorers, but their defensive record has repeatedly undermined their attacking performances. Parker acknowledged that committing players forward can leave his side exposed, particularly when possession changes hands, and stressed the importance of what his players do behind the ball.

Personally, I’ve always thought there were some relatively easy wins for Parker in terms of fixing West Ham’s defensive problems. We’re scoring plenty of goals; we just need to sort the defence out. And if there’s one thing Parker has demonstrated during his managerial career, it’s that he knows how to organise a team defensively.

During his time at Burnley, Parker oversaw one of the most remarkable defensive campaigns in English football history.

His side conceded just 16 goals across 46 Championship matches during the 2024/25 season, setting a upcoming record and keeping 30 clean sheets on their way to promotion.

Speaking in his talkSPORT interview, Parker discussed the importance of positioning when West Ham commit players forward, explaining that transitions and set pieces are particularly dangerous in the Championship.

And it’s interesting to hear him targeting transitions because that was exactly how West Ham conceded the opening goal against Blackburn Rovers in our last game.

Parker has informed West Ham players that they are now Championship players whether they like it or not.

But perhaps the most interesting part of Parker’s interview was his frank assessment of the mentality required from players who have dropped out of the Premier League.

He pointed out that the demands of the Championship are completely different, with players needing to accept the physical and psychological challenges of the division.

Parker then delivered a particularly pointed observation.

“If there’s a player here at this present moment in time playing in this division, it’s because that’s where he is.”.

It was a way of saying that irrespective of where you come from, it’s where you are that counts.

And no doubt there are players in the West Ham squad who consider themselves to be Premier League, European or international quality.

However, as of right now, they are Championship players, and Parker is quite right to point that out.

The upcoming gaffer has been promoted from this division three times, so I suspect he knows rather more about what is required than some of the players who have spent most of their careers in the Premier League.

Of course, the international break has given Parker a welcome opportunity to work with his players, although it’s vital to remember that ten were away representing their countries.

Nevertheless, he will have learned considerably more about those who remained at Rush Green.

In particular, players such as full-backs Ezra Mayers and Joël Veltman have had the opportunity to work with the newly introduced manager, while a good number of West Ham’s midfielders have also remained at the club.

That should have allowed Parker to concentrate on some of the defensive positioning and tactical habits he discussed during the interview.

And let’s not forget that he’ll also have Thursday and Friday’s training sessions to work with his returning internationals ahead of Preston.

That is considerably more preparation time than he enjoyed before his opening two matches against Cardiff and Blackburn.

The Fire finished fourth in the Eastern Conference this year, losing their last outing 4-3 to the Columbus Crew as they wound up a point above Charlotte, who drew 3-3 with Inter Miami on Decision Day.

Throughout 2026, Chicago were out to prove that last year was no fluke as they continued to improve in the league yet again.

In his second year as head coach, Gregg Berhalter saw his team gain two more points than in his inaugural campaign, while finishing four places higher in the Eastern Conference table this time around and making the playoffs on successive occasions.

The next step will be for the Fire to find some playoff success, with this club aiming to advance beyond the first round for the first time since 2009.

During this regular season campaign, they won three more home matches when compared to 2025, though they have only won one playoff fixture in Illinois since 2009, defeating Orlando City 3-1 in the Wildcard Round a year ago.

They have points in three of their last four MLS encounters but will try to snap a two-match domestic losing run at home this weekend, conceding a combined seven goals in those two defeats.

On Sunday, the Fire can beat Charlotte at home for a third consecutive occasion, having won those last two contests by a single goal.

The Crown are back in the post-season for a third successive occasion, hoping to get past round one at long last.

Dean Smith’s men set a single-season club record for goals scored in 2026 (66), averaging just under two per match (1.9) in the league this year.

This weekend, they will hope to end a four-match domestic winless run away from home and collect their first-ever road triumph in the post-season.

Defensively, they have been shaky as the visitors in 2026, conceding three or more goals on eight occasions in the regular season.

In round one of the playoffs, they have netted just one goal overall and have never scored in the opening half of an MLS road playoff game.

Charlotte have also never won a post-season game in normal time, and have scored first only once, in 2024 when they lost to Orlando City on penalties in the decisive third game of that best-of-three opening round series.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

West Ham United’s Championship promotion hopes may have received an unexpected boost following confirmation that Swansea City manager Vítor Matos has left the Welsh club to take charge of French side Strasbourg.

The Portuguese coach had established Swansea as genuine promotion contenders, with the Swans sitting sixth in the Championship. His departure comes at an awkward time for a club attempting to maintain its challenge near the top of the table.

Strasbourg officially appointed Matos on Wednesday evening, replacing Hugo Oliveira. And whilst there’s no guarantee Swansea will suffer without him, I certainly regard this as good news for West Ham.

Matos was an extremely capable manager who had Swansea punching well above their weight.

Industry observers note that when he arrived in November 2025, Swansea were languishing in 20th position. He eventually guided them to an 11th-place finish before establishing them amongst the promotion contenders this season.

I suspect they’ll drop off without him.

That remarked, with only one win in their last five matches, Swansea were struggling anyway. But I have little doubt this departure won’t help their cause.

Interestingly, Claret & Hugh reported last month that Matos could be targeted by Crystal Palace, highlighting how losing their manager could benefit West Ham’s promotion ambitions.

The destination has turned out to be Strasbourg rather than Selhurst Park, but the potential consequences for Swansea remain much the same.

From a West Ham perspective, I’ll certainly take it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By LEWIS STEELE, FOOTBALL REPORTER.

Published: 19:01 EST, 15 November 2026 | Updated: 08:25 EST, 16 November 2026.

Spending time in the tech giant of Neil Warnock is always an education, be it witnessing one of his legendary foul-mouthed touchline rants or perched at one of his stage shows at grand venues like London Palladium.

Recent findings suggest that on this occasion, Daily Mail Sport is perched in an east London bar watching on as one of English football's national treasures is posing for some modelling. Yes, you read that right, Mr Warnock is here to launch his own pair of socks with a tipple of Famous Grouse whisky in hand.

The complements on Warnock's 77-year-old feet are soon over, though, and we can get on to talking about a life in football that started six decades ago as a winger for Chesterfield and has traversed 10 clubs as a player, 17 as a manager and more than 2,000 games in the dugout.

Sources indicate that so where to start? Maybe his reflections on nearly five decades in management – and how the whole conversation about feet is not too out of place….

'You don't realise how long it has been really, I started off just a team of ragamuffins as I call them,' he says in his iconic Yorkshire accent. 'They used to train on the green where I had digs in Hartlepool and asked me to coach them.

It has been revealed that 'I remember we scored from a set-piece we worked on, I was running up and down the touchline high-fiving everyone. I got the bug. I knew I could never get to the top as a player, I was quick but I was brainless.

Daily Mail Sport caught up with Neil Warnock to discuss his six decades in football.

After representing 10 different clubs as a player, Warnock became one of the most compelling managers in the game.

'I could've been a chiropodist if not in football. That could be on a quiz, couldn't it? I had bad feet at Scunthorpe, I used to get massive blisters so the physio there started getting me to do some of the players' feet.

'I enjoyed doing ingrown toenails and things like that! So I thought why not? Then I had a practice in Sheffield. I had to make a decision when we won the league at Scarborough whether to go full-time or pack it in. I thought, "Oh, go on then, let's give it a little go".

'It's not worked out badly, really, has it?

'People come up to me every day and say, "You're a legend, you". And I say, "Oh, thank you very much". Then they tell me what club they support, I have had so many haven't I? Last week I went out for a minute and had four selfies. They all appreciate what I did for their club.

Sources indicate that 'There aren't as many characters in the game now, you wouldn't get upset with managers now like in my day because now they are that b****y boring! Some of them barely speak.

Industry observers note that 'They won't get the rapport we had. I managed at a good time. The way I managed, I needed that humour. I needed the lads to enjoy it. I signed a lot of players that many managers wouldn't touch with a barge pole, are you with me? They ended up getting me promotions.'.

The aforementioned humour brings us on to a private conversation he had with the great Pep Guardiola, one of the millions of anecdotes up Warnock's sleeve but one that he has not told until now.

'I went to a training session and he asked me to say a few words,' explains Warnock. 'I remarked, "Well lads I bet you're glad I'm not your manager because we'd be kicking balls from there to there, chasing it, heading it, practicing our tackles"... everyone laughed.

Warnock views Pep Guardiola as the best manager of his lifetime, while the Spaniard praised the veteran's humour after once addressing his Man City squad at a training session.

Warnock has led teams to promotions on eight occasions over the course of his career.

Industry observers note that 'After the session we had a coffee and Pep noted to me, "Neil, that was amazing, you know when you talked to the players? I understood why you had so many promotions".

'He started counting and stated, "What we have is all these staff… computers, details, nutritionist, all these staff, but you know what we don't have? Humour". He noticed why my lads had done well in my teams, just in that meeting. It was good, that. He is amazing.

According to recent reports, 'Pep is the best manager of my lifetime. They say he had all the best players but it is not easy managing them. Pep did things with players and now there are non-league teams trying to play like Manchester City!'.

Warnock is now doing stage tours - Guardiola attended one last season - and had a tear in his eye when he stepped out at London Palladium given he used to watch shows there with his mother, who was in a wheelchair, on the TV as a child.

So what is Warnock up to these days? His current role is advisor at Torquay United but last management job was at Aberdeen two years ago… so is he out of the rat race for good this time?

It has been revealed that 'No, not really, no,' he says. 'I only work from February to April! So the phone will be on after Christmas. You never know, do ya? There will be someone thinking "why don't we get that Warnock in?".

'I've retired 40 times! Every time I have noted it, I have meant it. But it's that dressing room camaraderie. There's something about football, when I look at some of the managers now… they just don't excite me.

In a recent development, 'I remember Ruben Amorim (breaks down laughing). He's got his computer out on the bench! I remember watching and thinking, "I'm sorry, son, you need more than a computer to help you tonight!".

Warnock is presently doing stage tours, with Guardiola among the attendees last season.

Warnock's current role is advisor at Torquay United and briefly served as interim manager last season, with the 77-year-old admitting he had not completely ruled out a return to the dugout.

'And likewise, I see them making notes on the bench, oh my god. I think "what are you doing, your shopping list for Tescos?".

Recent findings suggest that 'I do enjoy walking and I enjoy photography, believe it or not. I go up the river with my phone, there's so many lovely things to see.

'I've got an electric bike and I sometimes do about 25 miles. I was thinking of doing a cycle of all my clubs but that would take me five years! They go at about 30mph down the hills, you've got to be careful, you wouldn't want to come off them.'.

He is also enjoying fishing, being with the family and playing golf with his son, a PGA rising star William - though Warnock Sr insists he often embarrasses himself playing off 'the ladies' tee'.

The thing that makes Warnock most proud is the four promotions at Wembley but also the togetherness he fostered in his many teams.

Recent findings suggest that he tells us: 'What I like about the teams I had, they all have reunions. You look at the tele now, someone will score a goal and kiss the badge… they won't have a reunion.

'When I go to these reunions, I see all my lads and how I blended that dressing room together and I look at the comradeship they still have now, they are the same as they were just a lot older.

Recent findings suggest that 'This year, my Scarborough team are having a 40-year celebration and the lads have invited me. I said there's no way I'm going out with that lot after the do because they can drink, let me tell you!'.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent reports linking West Ham with Bristol City goalkeeper Joe Duncan are understandable. The 20-year-old has enjoyed an impressive loan spell at Southend United, earned a surprise senior Wales call-up and is attracting attention from a number of clubs.

But while Duncan is undoubtedly a talented young goalkeeper, West Ham must ask a simple question: why spend time, money and resources pursuing another developing keeper when they already have one of the country’s most highly-rated young goalkeepers sitting in their own academy?

Finlay Herrick joined the club at the age of six and has progressed through every level of the academy system. He was part of the famous side that won the FA Youth Cup and U18 Premier League South double in 2022/23, signed a long-term contract in 2024 and has represented England from U16 through to U20 level. Herrick, now aged 20, has already made three senior appearances for West Ham.

In a recent development, the standout moment came in the FA Cup quarter-final against Leeds United when he replaced Alphonse Areola in the 120th minute and immediately saved a penalty in the shootout. Although the Hammers ultimately lost, Herrick demonstrated the composure and personality required to perform under intense pressure.

He also acquitted himself well in the EFL second-round 4-1 win at Southampton back in August.

It has been revealed that in his last game, three saves, including a vital one-on-one against Fulham, were not enough as we were edged out of the EFL Cup 3-2 by our London rivals. However, our young custodian blamed himself for the third goal, saying he needed to be harsh on himself and should have done better to prevent it.

Sources indicate that regarding Duncan, he has come through Bristol City’s academy and gained valuable experience on loan at Tiverton Town and Farnborough before stepping up to National League football with Southend United. His performances have been good enough to earn a Wales senior squad call-up from Craig Bellamy despite never making a first-team appearance for Bristol City.

Southend manager Kieron Dyer and Bellamy have both spoken positively about his development, while West Ham are reportedly among several clubs monitoring his situation.

One of the biggest criticisms supporters have of modern football is that clubs often look elsewhere rather than trusting their own youth products. You only have to look at former academy prospect Nathan Trott, who was regularly loaned out to other clubs and has now swiftly established himself as the main keeper for Cardiff City.

Sources indicate that behind Herrick are a number of other keepers coming through the ranks, with high expectations of Lanre Awesu, who at just 18 years old has featured for the U21 side on a number of occasions. Standing at 6ft 5in, he has been highly praised by David Martin, along with fellow keeper Finley Hooper.

Herrick has already spent 14 years at the club. He has excelled at youth level, earned England recognition, performed well on loan and shown promise when given an opportunity with the senior side.

At some point, development becomes about opportunity.

Recent findings suggest that if a goalkeeper with Herrick’s pedigree cannot move up the pecking order, then what is the purpose of the academy pathway? What message does that give to Herrick, Awesu and Hooper?

With Hermansen failing to convince and Areola proving increasingly unreliable due to injuries, the moment for Herrick could arrive far quicker than anyone anticipated.

It has been revealed that in my opinion, the Hammers should show faith in their own. The smartest signing West Ham can make may already be wearing number 49 at Rush Green!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Sam Varley | 19 Nov 2026 23:37.

Aiming to break into the top eight of the Championship table on their return from the November international break, Sheffield United will welcome Watford to Bramall Lane on Saturday.

The hosts lost in their final game before the break but sit just two points outside of the playoff spots, while their visitors sit five points above the drop zone thanks to a win and a draw in their last two outings.

Sheffield United head back into Championship action after the international break on Saturday aiming to reignite their pursuit of the playoff places.

Aiming to kick on from a 13th-placed finish in 2025-26 and challenge for a return to the Premier League, the Blades experienced a mixed start to the season but looked to have turned a corner after the September and October break.

The Blades managed four wins and one draw in their first six games back from that break, scoring 11 goals and conceding six in those games, culminating in a 1-0 home victory over Wrexham, with Ben Brereton Diaz on the scoresheet, and a 3-2 away victory against Preston North End thanks to Sydie Peck's hat-trick.

They were unable to carry that winning streak into the latest break, though, visiting Charlton Athletic last time out and losing 2-1, having fallen behind and levelled through Jordan Ayew before Matt Godden scored the winner for their hosts 10 minutes from time.

Now sat 10th but just two points behind seventh and eighth spots, Sheffield United will again hope to come back firing and return to winning ways at Bramall Lane on Saturday.

Their visitors, meanwhile, head to South Yorkshire aiming to build on a positive turn in form before the break.

After a 16th-placed Championship finish in 2025-26 and the summer appointment of Alessio Dionisi, Watford endured a poor start to the new campaign, picking up just 11 points from their first 13 matches, winning three and losing eight of those.

The Hornets' away record is a real cause for concern, having lost six and drawn one of their seven league matches on the road, scoring just four goals in those and conceding 14.

The most recent of those was a 3-2 away loss against Norwich City, in which they led 2-0 at the break, but Dionisi's men did bounce back, beating Lincoln City 1-0 at home thanks to Stephy Mavididi's goal, before they hosted then-leaders Middlesbrough last time out and stood strong for a point from a 0-0 draw.

Watford now return to action hoping to add to those positive results and extend their five-point lead over the relegation zone.

Sheffield United Championship form:.

Sheffield Wednesday are unable to call on defender Femi Seriki, who sustained a long-term injury before the break, while Matt Doherty, Ryan One and Joe Rothwell may also remain sidelined.

Patrick Bamford may be in line for a return, though, having been out with a shoulder injury, and if deemed fit he could return up front from the start despite competition for those places from Ben Brereton Diaz, Tom Cannon, Jordan Ayew and Tyrese Campbell.

Kalvin Phillips has impressed in his second loan spell with the Blades thus far and will again join Sydie Peck in midfield.

Watford are still without Kwadwo Baah, Jeremy Ngakia, Soumaila Coulibaly and Edoardo Bove on Saturday due to ongoing injuries.

Kevin Keben and Branimir Mlacic should again join Mattie Pollock in the middle of the defence after their clean sheet against Middlesbrough last time out, while Krepin Diatta may start in a wing-back role if he is fit after being forced off in that game.

Competition for attacking spots is rife with Mamadou Doumbia, Amin Nabizada, Stephy Mavididi, Luca Kjerrumgaard, Rocco Vata and Othmane Maamma all pushing to start, while Myron Boadu has often led the line but missed the Middlesbrough game.

Sheffield United possible starting lineup:.

Cooper; Choudhury, Tanganga, Kitching, Burrows; Donovan, Peck, Phillips, Brereton Diaz; Cannon, Bamford.

Watford possible starting lineup:.

Ravaglia; Diatta, Keben, Pollock, Mlacic, Zemura; Kayembe, Kyprianou, Bravo; Mavididi, Doumbia.

Watford demonstrated signs of improvement before the break with consecutive clean sheets, but we fancy Sheffield United, rested after a disappointing defeat halted their notable improvement, to bounce back at Bramall Lane.

In a recent development, after a humiliating defeat by Grimsby Town in their previous League Cup campaign, Manchester United found a different way to exit the competition this time around. The jeers heard at the full-time whistle after throwing away a two-goal lead pointed to more worrying times a year on from Blundell Park.

For the first time in half a century, United lost a game at Old Trafford having led 2-0, highlighting the defensive problems Michael Carrick needs to solve after turning results around last season.

“What the f---ing hell was that?” shouted the home fans, in a chant that may have been aimed at the referee but equally applied to United’s players, who led through Shea Lacey and Mason Mount’s early goals.

According to recent reports, brighton cut through Carrick’s defence several times before staging their comeback with goals from Charalampos Kostoulas, Pascal Gross and Maxim De Cuyper. Carrick and his analysts will rewatch the footage of all three goals in horror at how they conceded.

Kostoulas halves the deficit! 🔵Brighton score on the stroke of half-time. pic.twitter.com/bGjN1w6s6c.

“I totally understand the feelings of the supporters,” Carrick remarked. “We have to accept it. I totally accept it. It’s on me ultimately: as a team what we look like, how we play and what results you get. I take that. I’ll take the praise, I’ll take the criticism and the upset.”.

Erik ten Hag used the domestic cups to taste success while struggling in the Premier League, but one of those opportunities is now lost to Carrick, who must be careful not to spiral from a poor start to the campaign into crisis. Sunday’s trip to Fulham before the international break now feels like a massive game for United and Carrick.

“We’ve gone out of the cup and the feeling around the place feels bigger than that,” Carrick said. “I’ll be honest about that, that’s how it feels, but it doesn’t have to be like that. If we win football matches again, it can go in a different direction.

According to recent reports, “We have a big game on Sunday that we have to prepare for. We’re out of this competition and we have to go back to winning football matches.

“It doesn’t feel good at the moment. It doesn’t feel good. We have to go back to winning football matches. We want to win and want to win swiftly. The next game is Sunday. That’s all I’m thinking about right now.”.

Sources indicate that at the start of the evening it seemed that the tie would be remembered for Lacey scoring on his first start for United, the first teenager to do so since Marcus Rashford. In the week when JJ Gabriel, one of United’s great academy talents, asked to leave the club, a different United teenager was kissing the badge when he found the net.

But Brighton’s way back into the game was to get Gross, 35, on the ball and the veteran German controlled the game.

Gross took his chance when United carelessly played the ball out of defence again, with Diogo Dalot’s clearance mishit. Luka Vuskovic’s header went straight into the United penalty area, with their centre-backs failing to react promptly enough.

Brighton have turned it around!!! 🔵A sensational comeback as Maxim De Cuyper makes it 3-2 at Old Trafford. pic.twitter.com/Bfcr4N7mTL.

Fabian Hürzeler’s side can be considered this season’s entertainers, with this comeback going with their seven-goal thriller against Chelsea, putting four past Aston Villa and five past Coventry at the weekend. Next for them in the League Cup is Manchester City or Norwich away, although they are unlikely to fear any opponents.

In a recent development, “We take it how it is. We want to go as far as possible but if you want to win something you have to win at the highest level,” Hürzeler noted. “We have to stay very, very humble and get an understanding why we are at the place we are and getting the basics right and the small margins right. It is so vital we stay humble and then we can grow into the game.”.

Recent findings suggest that for Carrick, matches such as this can define a United manager’s reign if he cannot turn results around. The image of Ruben Amorim in the dugout at Grimsby was one of the lasting impressions of last season before Carrick was brought in to salvage the campaign.

“We can’t put ourselves in that position after being ahead in the game and the game finishing like it did,” he stated. “So we’ve got to react to it. We’ve got another game on Sunday, we’ve got to react to it.”.

Industry observers note that boos ring around Old Trafford. Manchester United are out of the Carabao Cup, but of greater significance is that this defeat continues a poor start to the season and a general mood of deflation around the club. For the first time in 50 years, they lose a game at Old Trafford after leading 2-0. Another proud record falls in the post-Ferguson era.

Brighton have now won five of their last six games at Old Trafford, and are one of the best front-footed sides in the league on form.

As United push everyone forward, Heaven is penalised for a push on Vuskovic, and that is surely that now.

Five minutes of added time to play, but Brighton have a corner after their press ensnares Tielemans on the edge of United’s defensive third. Dalot got a toe to the ball to prevent Rutter a sight at goal. Darlow claims the delivery, but some time has ticked away.

Tielemans slices his cross over the bar while off balance. This would be the first time since 1976 that United have led 2-0 in a game at Old Trafford and gone on to lose. At the moment, an equaliser does not look to be on its way.

Old Trafford growing impatient with how slowly United are moving the ball, a lack of options for the player in possession and they are being caught on it repeatedly by a sharp Brighton team.

Breaking: Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer’s disease

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 94 min read (18724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~94 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration1,2.
  • Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is an age-associated neurodegenerative disease affecting millions worldwide, with a prevalence of roughly 10–30% among individuals older than 65 years3.
  • The hypothalamus, a small but complex brain region, orchestrates a wide range of physiological and neuroendocrine processes frequently dysregulated in ageing and AD2,7.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration1,2. These fundamental processes are regulated by the hypothalamus, yet how its functionally distinct subregions and cell types change during human ageing and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) remains largely unexplored. Here we present HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, including high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei from young participants, patients with AD and age-matched non-dementia control participants. We show that hypothalamic subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian rhythms are particularly vulnerable, showing notable changes in both volumes and gene expression during ageing and AD. At the molecular level, machine learning models identified the inflammatory response and regulators of circadian rhythms as key cellular predictors of AD. These signatures were reflected in specific cell types: microglia transitioned to a pro-inflammatory state, whereas inhibitory neurons within sleep-regulating and circadian-regulating hypothalamic subregions showed the most profound transcriptional alterations, including disruptions in ligand–receptor interactions and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling. HypoAD provides a high-resolution volumetric map and a transcriptomic atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, relating lifestyle and behavioural changes to the relevant volumetric and molecular pathways. In addition, HypoAD provides a framework to investigate hypothalamic dysfunction and establishes a roadmap for targeted interventions aimed at mitigating physiological disruptions to potentially slow disease progression.

Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is an age-associated neurodegenerative disease affecting millions worldwide, with a prevalence of roughly 10–30% among individuals older than 65 years3. Although its cardinal feature is cognitive impairment, AD manifests as a systemic condition involving profound disruptions in sleep, circadian rhythms, metabolic homeostasis, stress responses and neuroendocrine functions1. The canonical neuropathological hallmarks are extracellular amyloid-β plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs), which alongside widespread neuroinflammation and volumetric brain changes, also intensify with ageing1,4. Because cognitive decline has traditionally guided both diagnosis and research, investigation has focused mainly on the hippocampus and cortex5. As the effects of AD on other brain regions remain poorly understood, investigating these understudied areas is crucial for elucidating the full spectrum of disease mechanisms and developing fresh therapeutics6.

The hypothalamus, a small but complex brain region, orchestrates a wide range of physiological and neuroendocrine processes frequently dysregulated in ageing and AD2,7. Emerging evidence suggests that hypothalamic dysfunction not only correlates with but also actively exacerbates AD pathology and cognitive decline1. Specifically, pathology within hypothalamic subregions, such as the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)8, arcuate nucleus (ARC)1,9 and mammillary body10, has been associated with prominent sleep disturbances, metabolic dysfunction and memory deficits observed in patients with AD. These systemic disruptions, in turn, are proposed to create a vicious cycle that further accelerates disease progression and cognitive decline1.

Sources indicate that despite its central role in homeostasis and brain ageing2,11, the hypothalamus remains an understudied region in the context of human ageing and AD. In particular, we have a limited understanding of the volumetric, cellular and molecular changes within the human hypothalamus during these processes. Although studies in animal models have highlighted hypothalamic involvement in ageing and neurodegeneration2,11,12, human studies remain scarce. This may be in part because the hypothalamus is more evolutionarily conserved than the cortex and is critical for survival, and thus it may show less overt vulnerability to ageing and prevalent diseases13. This paucity is especially pronounced for investigations that combine high-resolution imaging with single-cell analyses, complementary approaches essential for dissecting the anatomical and cellular heterogeneity of this complex brain region. This knowledge gap hinders our ability to determine how specific hypothalamic subregions and cell populations contribute to ageing and AD, and why they show differential vulnerability.

Here we present HypoAD, a multimodal atlas combining two powerful, cross-scale approaches. First, we performed high-resolution volumetric analysis of clinical imaging data from 458 individuals across the adult lifespan with varying cognitive and amyloid-β pathological statuses. Second, we generated a complementary single-cell transcriptomic atlas, comprising 614,403 nuclei from the hypothalami of 17 post-mortem donors, including young and older individuals with or without clinical and neuropathological diagnoses of AD, in which sampling was specifically enriched for the SCN, ARC and mammillary body. This dual-modality approach reveals the subregion-specific and cell-type-specific alterations of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD.

Neuroimaging studies have reported changes in hypothalamic volumes associated with ageing and cognitive decline14. Previous analyses were low-resolution or limited to major areas, masking disease-relevant subregions such as the ARC and SCN14. To overcome this limitation, we leveraged a newly developed volumetric atlas of the human hypothalamus15 to delineate and measure 13 hypothalamic and 12 extrahypothalamic structures (Supplementary Table 1). Our analysis included a clinical imaging dataset of 458 individuals across two previously described cohorts: the Adult Metabolism & Brain Resilience (AMBR) study16 (n = 202) and the Connectomics in Brain Aging and Dementia (CBA) study17 (n = 256) (Extended Data Fig. 1a).

Pearson correlation analysis revealed that whereas total hypothalamic volume highlighted a weak correlation with age (r = 0.15, adjusted P = 1.5 × 10 −3, Fig. 1a, Supplementary Table 2), its constituent subregions showed stronger age-related correlations. Specifically, the lateral hypothalamus volume was negatively correlated with age (r = −0.22, adjusted P = 5.2 × 10−6), suggesting age-related atrophy. By contrast, the volumes of the SCN (r = 0.26, adjusted P = 2.8 × 10−8), ARC (r = 0.32, adjusted P = 1.7 × 10−11), paraventricular nucleus (r = 0.35, adjusted P = 6.9 × 10−14), periventricular nucleus (r = 0.34, adjusted P = 8.8 × 10−13) and dorsomedial hypothalamic nucleus (DMH) (r = 0.23, adjusted P = 1.8 × 10−6) all increased with age across all 458 individuals in two studies: AMBR and CBA (Fig. 1a,b and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3). A few subregions (SCN, mammillary body, dorsal periventricular nucleus and tuberomammillary nucleus) showed lower test–retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) < 0.4; Extended Data Fig. 1b), probably reflecting their small size and limited tissue contrast; volumetric results for these subregions should therefore be interpreted with caution. In the AMBR cohort the positive correlation between DMH volume and age was not detected in cognitively normal, amyloid-β negative individuals (Extended Data Fig. 1c,d and Supplementary Tables 2 and 3), but it remained present in the larger harmonized two-study cohort (n = 458; Extended Data Fig. 1c,d). To test whether this age-related increase in DMH volume itself differs by disease status, an age × group interaction model (group: cognitively normal and amyloid-negative versus all others; Methods) showed no significant interaction (effect size/estimate ± standard error (s.e.) = −0.041 ± 0.025, adjusted P = 0.12, Supplementary Table 4), indicating that age-related increase in DMH volume does not differ significantly between groups. This suggests that the DM–age association probably reflects a general feature of hypothalamic ageing in this subregion—which is implicated in sleep–wakefulness18 and body-weight regulation19—rather than a process specific to neurodegeneration.

Industry observers note that in a generalized linear model (GLM) controlling for biological sex, intracranial volume (ICV), cognitive status and amyloid-β pathology, lateral hypothalamus volume decreased with age (effect size/estimate ± s.e. = −0.021 ± 0.0064, adjusted P = 0.0019). The SCN (0.059 ± 0.018, adjusted P = 0.0029), ARC (0.058 ± 0.012, adjusted P = 4.2 × 10−6), paraventricular nucleus (0.14 ± 0.019, adjusted P = 1.8 × 10−11), periventricular nucleus (0.092 ± 0.019, adjusted P = 6.4 × 10−6), DMH (0.055 ± 0.016, adjusted P = 0.0011) and total hypothalamic volumes (0.022 ± 0.0071, adjusted P = 0.0048) highlighted a positive association with age (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 4). Biological sex was also a significant factor: females showed smaller volumes in several subregions, most prominently in the supraoptic nucleus (−0.097 ± 0.019, adjusted P = 1.7 × 10−6) (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 4). This aligns with previous studies emphasizing the sexually dimorphic nature of the hypothalamus, including the supraoptic nucleus2,14. As expected, most subregion volumes were positively correlated with ICV (Extended Data Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 4). For comparison, volumes of most extrahypothalamic structures showed age-related reductions, smaller sex differences than the hypothalamus and positive correlations with ICV (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 4). Representative subregions were reconstructed in three dimensions (Fig. 1d).

To holistically evaluate volumetric relationships, we performed principal component analysis (PCA) on volumetric data from all 25 delineated hypothalamic and extrahypothalamic structures (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 3a–e). The first two principal components (PCs) were primarily associated with age, sex and global scaling factors (intracranial and total brain volume), along which individuals separated (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 3a). Amyloid-β and cognitive status highlighted weaker associations with these components, and after residualizing for age, sex and global scaling factors, neither remained significantly associated with the leading PCs (Fig. 1e and Extended Data Fig. 3a–e). This indicates that disease status does not define an independent dominant axis of macrostructural variation, and that the more sensitive disease-associated signal may instead be captured at the molecular level.

Examination of volumetric trajectories by means of scatter plots stratified by cognitive and amyloid-β status revealed subregion-specific patterns that also differed by sex (Fig. 1f and Extended Data Fig. 3f). Notably, individuals with AD (defined as cognitive decline and amyloid-β positivity) highlighted reduced total hypothalamus and lateral hypothalamus volumes compared with their age-matched non-AD counterparts, consistent with the overall age-related decline of these regions (Extended Data Fig. 3g). By contrast, ARC, SCN, paraventricular nucleus, periventricular nucleus and DMH volumes were increased in individuals with AD relative to age-matched non-AD individuals (Extended Data Fig. 3g). This pattern did not reach statistical significance, potentially reflecting the insensitivity of volumetric measures to the relatively early disease stage and the limited sample size (Extended Data Fig. 3g). Subregion volumes classified cognitive status, amyloid-β status and AD better than total hypothalamic volume (Extended Data Fig. 3h,i), suggesting that subregion-specific volumetric changes capture disease-relevant variation that is obscured when the hypothalamus is treated as a single structure.

Thus, ageing is associated with subregion-specific volumetric changes that persist after controlling for amyloid-β and cognition, whereas AD-linked changes did not reach significance, motivating a complementary, higher-resolution molecular modality.

Industry observers note that volumetric data provide anatomical context but cannot reveal cell-type-specific molecular changes. We therefore performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) on post-mortem hemi-hypothalamus tissue from 14 individuals (Fig. 2a,b and Extended Data Fig. 4a): seven with mostly early-stage AD (n = 6 sporadic, n = 1 familial) and seven age-matched, cognitively and neuropathologically normal control participants. The familial AD sample (AD_44, ID 7A in Fig. 2b; APOE4/4) was excluded from all differential analyses and retained as an extreme example of advanced pathology.

It has been revealed that a, Schematic of the snRNA-seq workflow. Frozen post-mortem hypothalamic tissue from 14 individuals (7 non-AD control participants and 7 patients with AD (6 age-matched sporadic and 1 younger familial)) was macrodissected to enrich for the ARC, SCN and mammillary nucleus (MN) subregions. Nuclei were isolated, and libraries were prepared and sequenced on a NovaSeq platform. The resulting data were integrated with 133,879 publicly available nuclei from three young, healthy control participants, yielding a final dataset of 614,403 nuclei across young control, older control (non-AD) and AD groups for comparative analysis. b, Overview of the 14 individuals included in the snRNA-seq study, detailing sample IDs, clinical condition (non-AD control, early-stage AD or familial AD), age at death and Braak stage. Each individual contributed tissue from three hypothalamic subregions (ARC, SCN and MN), totalling 42 tissue samples processed across seven experimental batches. c, UMAP plot of the integrated 614,403 nuclei. Distinct clusters represent identified main cell types, including neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, endothelial cells, ependymal cells, fibroblasts, epithelial cells, OPCs and leukocytes. Each cell type is annotated and highlighted with a unique colour. d, Dot plot of selected marker genes. Dot size corresponds to the fraction of cells within a given cell type expressing the marker; colour intensity indicates the average normalized expression level. e, Normalized expression of key canonical marker genes mapped onto the UMAP plot from c. Representative markers include GFAP (astrocytes), FLT1 (endothelial cells), CFAP299 (ependymal cells), TTR (epithelial cells), C1QA (microglia), PTPRC/CD45 (leukocytes), SYT1 (neurons), MBP (oligodendrocytes), VCAN (OPCs) and COL1A1 (fibroblasts). Sources indicate that donors with AD predominantly had sporadic, clinically confirmed cognitive decline with pathology (Braak stage IV; Fig. 2b), a stage optimal for detecting transcriptional changes while neuronal populations remain20. Hierarchical clustering grouped samples by pathology status rather than by confounders such as time of death or quality metrics (Extended Data Fig. 4a).

In a recent development, for annotation, we integrated our dataset with 133,879 previously published, high-quality human hypothalamic nuclei from three younger individuals (29, 42 and 50 years of age)21,22 using the single-cell variational inference algorithm23. Main cell types were identified through the expression of canonical marker genes (Fig. 2c–e and quality control in Extended Data Fig. 4b–g).

To identify transcriptomic features distinguishing hypothalamic cells from patients with AD versus control individuals, we trained Elastic Net models on 36,600 genes from 480,524 cells. The dataset spanned seven independent batches, each containing one donor with AD and one control donor (Fig. 3a). This balanced design enabled a leave-one-batch-out cross-validation that yielded strong classification performance for both the all-cell model and cell-type-specific models for the main cell types (Fig. 3b).

In a recent development, averaging absolute gene weights across the seven outer cross-validation folds gave the top 20 features per classifier (Fig. 3c), many previously implicated in AD pathology, lending biological support to our model’s predictions. The all-cell model’s top features included arginine–vasopressin (encoded by AVP), a circadian neuropeptide elevated in AD24. Cell-type-specific models likewise highlighted AD-linked genes: MCF2L (differentially methylated in AD; oligodendrocyte)25, ARL17B (an inhibitory neuron expression quantitative trait locus elevated in AD cortex; neurons)26, CHI3L1 (astrocyte-secreted neuroinflammation marker and a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarker for early AD diagnosis; astrocytes)27, RNF150 (a cis-expression quantitative trait locus, microglia)28 and ITGA8 (linked to demyelination; oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC))29 (Fig. 3c).

According to recent reports, ranking genes by mean rank across the five most abundant cell types identified HP1BP3 as the top shared feature (Fig. 3d), a candidate modulator of hippocampal cognitive ageing affected by metformin30,31 but underexplored in the hypothalamus. A per-gene specificity rank (Fig. 3e) revealed strong enrichment of long noncoding RNAs (for example, LINC02646, LINC00551, LINC01250, LINC00937 and LINC02389) among top neuronal features (Fig. 3e), providing a cell-type-specific resource of known and newly introduced AD-associated genes. Gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA) on the ranked predictive genes revealed a significant enrichment for circadian rhythm and inflammatory pathways (Fig. 3f, Extended Data Fig. 5 and Supplementary Table 5), connecting our cell-level classifiers to established hallmarks of neurodegeneration.

Notably, microglia highlighted the largest number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs), highlighting their substantial transcriptional response even in early AD.

It has been revealed that for orthogonal validation, we leveraged a human CSF proteome dataset from healthy control participants and individuals with AD. Among the significantly differentially abundant proteins (Supplementary Table 7), five corresponded to significant DEGs across main cell types, three in endothelial cells, a primary component of the blood–brain barrier (Extended Data Fig. 6a): increased hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HPRT) and decreased brain-derived neurotrophic factor and neuropeptide Y. These align with blood–brain barrier dysfunction as an early AD feature32, reduced brain-derived neurotrophic factor and neuropeptide Y reflecting loss of neuroprotection33,34 and elevated HPRT suggesting the purine-salvage stress response35. Microglial PGK1 upregulation indicates a glycolytic shift characteristic of pro-inflammatory microglia36,37. PTPRN points to an altered OPC state38. GSEA on microglial DEGs revealed enrichment for G2M checkpoint, mTORC1 signalling and cholesterol homeostasis. These findings suggest that in early AD, microglia may enter a complex, supportive state. The mTORC1 signature points to metabolic reprogramming, and the cholesterol homeostasis signature is consistent with enhanced cholesterol efflux linked to amyloid-β phagocytosis, together suggesting an early supportive microglial response (Fig. 4b).

Because cellular senescence contributes to ageing and neurodegeneration39, we scored three senescence signatures—Canonical senescence, Senescence responses and Senescence initiators (Fig. 4c)—alongside three overlapping NFT signatures39 (Extended Data Fig. 6b–d and Supplementary Table 8), across cell types. Microglia, leukocytes, fibroblasts and endothelial cells demonstrated the highest scores, elevated with both ageing (control) and AD (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 6b–d), whereas neuronal NFT was most pronounced in the patient with APOE4/4 familial AD (AD_44) (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 6b–d). These findings suggest a dichotomy: senescence in non-neuronal cells may contribute to microenvironmental dysfunction in AD, whereas neuronal NFTs reflect a distinct, tau-driven pathology that escalates with disease progression or genetic susceptibility. This highlights the potential for different, cell-type-specific therapeutic targets. To ask whether these transcriptomic changes could relate to the subregion volume changes seen by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), we examined pathways regulating cell size and tissue architecture. A curated mTOR signalling gene set (core regulators MTOR, RPTOR, RHEB, TSC1/2 and DEPTOR; effectors RPS6KB1, EIF4EBP1 and SREBF1/2) showed an increased module score in AD, most prominently in non-neuronal cells (Extended Data Fig. 6e and Supplementary Table 9). Because mTORC1 regulates cell growth and size40, this raises cellular hypertrophy as one speculative contributor to the volume increases observed at the macrostructural level. Conversely, an extracellular matrix (ECM) gene set (collagens COL1A1 and COL4A1; proteoglycans ACAN, BCAN and VCAN; glycoproteins SPARC,and TNC) showed a decreased module score in AD (Extended Data Fig. 6f and Supplementary Table 9). These shifts suggest cell-size regulation and extracellular remodelling as candidate molecular processes potentially relevant to the subregion volume changes.

Microglia are central to brain ageing and neurodegeneration11,41,42. We applied trajectory inference43,44 to microglia from all conditions (young, older control participants and AD), inferring a continuous ageing-to-AD trajectory (Fig. 4d, Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Table 10). The pseudotime continuum was categorized into four stages: ageing phases of microglia from young participants (stage 1) and older control participants (stage 2), a late ageing phase enriched for older control participants (stage 3, representing a later state for these cells along the trajectory) and AD (stage 4) microglia (Fig. 4e and Extended Data Fig. 7a–e). A subset of microglia from older control individuals appeared at earlier trajectory points, whereas some microglia from young individuals persisted into later stages, suggesting that certain microglia may retain youthful properties whereas others show heightened susceptibility to early pathological changes.

Sources indicate that we scored three microglial signatures with UCell45 across pseudotime: (1) homeostatic (CSF1R and CX3CR1); (2) stage 1 disease-associated microglia (DAM1) (APOE and B2M), which are typically activated by ageing and amyloid plaques and (3) stage 2 DAM (DAM2) (AXL and CLEC7A), which are dependent on TREM2 signalling46,47. The scores revealed a transition from homeostatic towards DAM1 with a modest DAM2 rise (Fig. 4e,f), some of which were validated in the CSF proteomics data (Extended Data Fig. 7f). This observed shift from homeostatic-to-DAM states underscores the critical role of microglial functional changes in AD progression and highlights the potential for therapeutic interventions aimed at preserving homeostatic functions or preventing the full transition to detrimental DAM states.

Moran’s I test identified 13,104 trajectory-associated DEGs (t-DEGs) (Supplementary Table 11 and Extended Data Fig. 7g), smoothed with RVAgene48 and clustered (Fig. 4g). Gene Ontology biological process analysis of these t-DEGs revealed that the ageing phase shifts from cilium assembly and mitochondrial morphogenesis towards stress responses, including amyloid precursor protein catabolic processes, and the disease phase shifts from cell morphogenesis and synaptic modulation to viral response pathways and protein targeting to the endoplasmic reticulum (Fig. 4h).

Sources indicate that to test generalization beyond our cohort and the hypothalamus, we compared against the PsychAD single-nucleus atlas of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex49,50. AD-associated expression was directionally concordant across non-neuronal cell types and strongest in glia, whereas endothelial cells highlighted more region-specific changes consistent with the distinct vascular microenvironment of the hypothalamus (Extended Data Fig. 8a and Supplementary Table 12). In two independent PsychAD cohorts (ageing, 208 donors49; AD, 585 donors)50, DAM signatures rose with age and AD status, recapitulating our homeostatic-to-DAM progression (Extended Data Fig. 8b–g and Supplementary Table 13). Together, these cross-cohort, cross-region comparisons indicate that the main transcriptomic signatures identified in the HypoAD hypothalamus are reproducible in independently generated datasets.

Sources indicate that neurons in the human hypothalamus show extensive cell-type diversity13,21,22. We analysed 213,469 neuronal nuclei, classifying them into three neurotransmitter-defined categories: inhibitory and/or γ-aminobutyric acid-ergic (GABAergic) (GAD2), excitatory and/or glutamatergic (SLC17A6) and histaminergic neurons (HDC) (Fig. 5a–c). Hierarchical Leiden clustering yielded five levels of clustering (5 to 254 subclusters). Anatomical origin was inferred from curated subregional markers21 (Extended Data Fig. 9a), with the dominant subregion listed first for subclusters expressing several markers (Extended Data Fig. 9a). A dendrogram related subtypes across resolutions, with nodes and leaves labelled by distinguishing markers. The 254 leaf subclusters were annotated by relative abundance within the total neuronal population, their distribution across young participants, older control participants and patients with AD, and inferred subregion (Fig. 5d).
