We also genetically ablated p38α in Gpx4−/− MC38 cells, which disabled ferroptosis-induced PGE2 production (Extended Data Fig. 9c) and resulted in enhanced tumour growth control in WT mice (Extended Data Fig. 9d), consistent with the idea that p38 MAPK-induced PGE2 production by ferroptotic tumours promotes immune escape.

Recent findings suggest that of note, the efficient elimination of Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice was linked to markedly increased intratumoural numbers of CXCL9-producing cDC1s (Fig. 4c), indicating their enhanced anticancer activity. By contrast, the numbers of CXCL9-producing cDC1s remained low in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in WT mice, and in WT MC38 tumours in both WT and Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice (Fig. 4c). Confocal immunofluorescence microscopy further revealed a prominent increase of interactive clusters between cDC1s and CD8+ TILs in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice (Extended Data Fig. 9e,f), pointing towards more productive cDC1-mediated instruction of anticancer CD8+ TIL responses19,26. Consistently, CD8+ TILs displayed substantially enhanced expansion in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice compared with all other groups (Fig. 4d,e).

cDC1s fulfil an essential role in anticancer immunity by driving the expansion and effector differentiation of TCF1+CD8+ TILs (often referred to as ‘stem-like’ T cells) into TIM3+(TCF1−)CD8+ TILs with cytotoxic effector functions26. In many tumours, this process is critical for protective anticancer immunity37,38,39,40. The CD8+ TILs selectively accumulating in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice predominantly encompassed TIM3+(TCF1−)CD8+ TILs (Fig. 4f and Extended Data Fig. 10a) with high PD-1 and CXCR6 expression (Extended Data Fig. 10a), indicating more productive effector differentiation20,40. Consistently, TIM3+ TILs in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice showed markedly increased frequencies of cells expressing the cytotoxic effector molecule granzyme B (GZMB) compared with all other groups (Fig. 4g,h). We also confirmed that the numbers of stem-like TCF1+ TILs were comparable across all groups (Extended Data Fig. 10b), consistent with their unaffected tumour infiltration.

Of note, the few TIM3+CD8+ TILs detectable in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in WT mice, similar to Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice, displayed high expression of the proliferation marker Ki-67 (Fig. 4i and Extended Data Fig. 10c). This result indicates that CD8+ TILs, at least to some degree, mount proliferative responses also in ferroptotic tumours in the presence of intact PGE2 signalling on cDC1s. However, profiling of CD8+ TILs at later stages demonstrated that, in Gpx4−/− tumours in WT mice, these responses are not sustained over time, both in terms of Ki-67 expression, GZMB expression and CD8+ TIL expansion (Extended Data Fig. 10d–f). By contrast, CD8+ TIL responses in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice in Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours further increased over time (Extended Data Fig. 10d–f). Thus, only Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice, but not WT mice, can mount protective CD8+ T cell immunity against ferroptotic tumours. By antibody-mediated CD8+ T cell depletion, we further confirmed the relevance of CD8+ T cells for elimination of ferroptotic Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice (Extended Data Fig. 10g–i).

In a recent development, finally, to specifically examine whether pharmacological inhibition of COX-driven PGE2 production can achieve better immune control of ferroptotic tumours, we analysed the growth of Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours transplanted into WT mice with or without CXB treatment. In line with PGE2-mediated impairment of anticancer immunity against ferroptotic tumours, Gpx4−/− MC38 tumours in CXB-treated mice displayed markedly increased control of tumour growth (Fig. 4j). Of note, this effect was associated with prominently enhanced expansion of CD8+ TILs (Fig. 4k), with a high frequency of GZMB-expressing cells (Extended Data Fig. 10j). Similarly, tumours formed by Gpx4−/− BRAF(V600E) melanoma cells exhibited tumour regression in CXB-treated, but not in untreated, WT mice (Extended Data Fig. 10k). Consistent with these data, BRAF(V600E) melanoma tumour-bearing WT mice treated with a combination of CXB and the ferroptosis inducer imidazole ketone erastin (IKE) displayed enhanced tumour growth control compared with untreated mice or mice treated with CXB or IKE alone (Fig. 4l and Extended Data Fig. 10l). Together, these data suggest that PGE2 produced by ferroptotic cancer cells limits anticancer immunity by controlling cDC1-driven effector differentiation and expansion of CD8+ TILs, which enables ferroptotic tumours to escape immune control. Interfering with the PGE2–EP2/EP4 axis can elicit cDC1-mediated expansion and effector differentiation of CD8+ TILs in ferroptotic tumours and result in protective anticancer immunity.

In a recent development, our results demonstrate that ferroptosis in cancer cells triggers aberrant synthesis of the bioactive lipid PGE2, enabling ferroptotic cancer cells to exert deleterious effects on cDC1-dependent, CD8+ TIL-mediated anticancer immunity within tumour tissue. This inhibitory mechanism is critical for immune escape of ferroptotic tumours.

It has been revealed that beyond highlighting that tumour ferroptosis causes suppression of anticancer immunity, as has been recently suggested8,9,10,14,17, our results reveal that this barrier to ferroptosis-inducing strategies mechanistically depends on PGE2 and its signalling through the PGE2 receptors EP2 and EP4, preventing cDC1-mediated expansion and effector differentiation of anticancer CD8+ TILs. As a result, interference with PGE2–EP2/EP4 signalling enhances the anticancer activity of cDC1s in ferroptotic tumours and induces protective, CD8+ TIL-mediated anticancer immunity. These findings therefore identify a molecular mechanism fundamentally linked to the metabolic underpinnings of ferroptosis that may be decisive for ferroptosis-mediated impairment of cancer immunity. Of note, it seems likely that PGE2 from ferroptotic tumour cells not only targets cDC1s but in parallel also interferes directly with anticancer TILs, as indicated by our data. PGE2 may further limit the anticancer activity of other innate immune cells such as type 2 conventional DCs (cDC2s), monocyte–macrophages or natural killer cells41.

Recent findings suggest that we have revealed that PGE2 production by ferroptotic cancer cells involves p38 MAPK signalling activated through lipid peroxidation-induced, membrane permeabilization-dependent Ca2+ influx, which activates a molecular program that causes transcriptional upregulation of the COX–PGE2 pathway. Beyond providing a mechanistic explanation for high COX2 levels in ferroptotic cells, as has been recently observed18,42, our results uncover that this trait acquired by ferroptotic cells is uncoupled from the execution of cell death. As a consequence, interference with p38 MAPK signalling can disable the production of PGE2 while maintaining effective cancer cell elimination by ferroptosis inducers.

In a recent development, multiple studies have highlighted the vulnerability of therapy-resistant and difficult-to-treat cancers to ferroptosis induction and the dependency of ferroptotic cancer elimination on anticancer immunity. Therefore, our discoveries that ferroptotic tumour cells antagonize anticancer immunity through the PGE2–EP2/EP4 axis and the uncoupling of this mechanism from ferroptosis-mediated tumour cell elimination have crucial mechanistic and clinical implications. Our results indicate that targeting PGE2–EP2/EP4 signalling to overcome ferroptosis-induced immunosuppression may provide an attractive means to unleash anticancer CD8+ T cell immunity and achieve cancer elimination by ferroptosis-inducing strategies. On this note, abolishing PGE2 production by inhibition of p38 MAPK signalling bears the potential to interfere with the immunosuppressive capacity of ferroptotic cancer cells without curbing ferroptosis-mediated cancer cell elimination. Our findings therefore identify p38 MAPK signalling-induced COX–PGE2 pathway activity in ferroptotic cancer cells as a potential molecular target to prevent immune evasion and improve cancer therapy by ferroptosis-inducing strategies. Of note, disabling the p38 MAPK–COX–PGE2 signalling may further benefit necroptosis-inducing strategies, as indicated by our findings with necroptotic cells.

All mice used in this study were on a C57BL/6J genetic background and obtained from Jackson Laboratory (JAX). Ptger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice were generated by crossing Ptger2−/− mice (004376, JAX) to Ptger4fl/fl mice (028102, JAX) and further crossed to Clec9acre mice (025523, JAX) to generate Clec9acrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice, crossed to Cd4cre mice (022071, JAX) to generate Cd4crePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice or crossed to Itgaxcre mice (008068, JAX) to generate ItgaxcrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl mice. OT-I × CD45.1 mice were generated by crossing OT-I mice (003831, JAX) to CD45.1 (002014, JAX) mice. Unless stated otherwise, all mice used in this study were used on a CD45.2/CD45.2 background. In all experiments, mice at 8–20 weeks of age were sex matched and randomly assigned to control or treatment groups. Mouse tumour experiments with Gpx4−/− tumours as well as T cell depletion were conducted without blinding; all other experiments were conducted in a blinded manner. No statistical methods were used to predetermine sample sizes. Mice were killed by cervical dislocation under anaesthesia. All mice were maintained and bred at the Technical University of Munich Klinikum rechts der Isar, under specific-pathogen-free, standard conditions with water and food ad libitum, in a controlled environment (22 ± 2 °C, 55 ± 10% humidity, 12 h light–dark cycle) and in accordance with the guidelines of the Federation of European Laboratory Animal Science Associations. All animal experiments were performed in accordance with the guidelines of the District Government of Upper Bavaria (Department 5–Environment, Health and Consumer Protection).

Control and Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E) melanoma cells were generated using the CRISPR–Cas9 system as previously described21. BRAF(V600E)–OVA and Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E)–OVA variants were generated by lentiviral transduction, as previously described20. 4-OH-TAM-inducible Gpx4−/− mouse immortalized fibroblasts (Pfa1) have been previously described43. Gpx4−/− MC38 and Gpx4−/− BRAF(V600E) cells were generated by CRISPR–Cas9-mediated gene editing using the lentiCRISPR v2-puro vector expressing single guide RNAs, as previously described44. In brief, Gpx4-targeting single guide RNA (5′-caccGCGTGTGCATCGTCACCAACG) was cloned in the BsmBI-digested lentiCRISPR v2-puro vector (98290, Addgene) and used to transiently transfect cancer cell lines using the X-tremeGENE HP agent (Roche). One day after transfection, cells were selected using puromycin (5 µg ml−1) and further cultivated with Lip-1 (1 µM) to prevent ferroptosis. After selection, single-cell clones were picked, and knockout clones were identified by immunoblotting. Mapk14−/− cells were generated by CRISPR–Cas9-mediated gene editing using the p38α MAPK14 CRISPR–Cas9 knockout plasmid (sc-424051; Santa Cruz) according to manufacturer’s protocol. After sorting for GFP+ cells, single-cell clones were picked, and knockout clones were identified by immunoblotting. Pfa1, Lewis lung carcinoma (LLC) and Gpx4−/− LLC cells were provided by M.C.; MC38 and Su86.86 cells were provided by A. Krüger. small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) cell lines were provided by S.v.K.

According to recent reports, BRAF(V600E), Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E), BRAF(V600E)–OVA, Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E)–OVA, 4T1, NRAS(G12D), LLC, CT26, SLCL, Pfa1, NIH3T3, A549, Su86.86 and HT-29 cells were cultured in complete RPMI medium (RPMI 1640 medium, Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 10% FCS (PAN-Biotech), 50 U ml–1 penicillin (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 50 µg ml–1 streptomycin (Thermo Fisher Scientific). MC38, D4M.3 A, Panc02, mouse pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and human patient-derived PDAC cells were cultured in DMEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 10% FCS, 50 U ml–1 penicillin and 50 mg ml–1 streptomycin. Gpx4−/− cells were cultured in their respective medium supplemented with 1 μM Lip-1 to prevent ferroptosis. For in vitro assays, Gpx4−/− cell lines were cultivated in 1 µM Ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) for one passage before seeding them with or without Fer-1 to assess ferroptosis and PGE2 production. Unless stated otherwise, all analyses of cell viability and PGE2 production were performed after 24 h.

According to recent reports, to generate cancer cell conditioned medium, 4 × 105 cancer cells were cultured in 2 ml complete RPMI medium or DMEM for 24 h before addition of the ferroptosis inducers RSL3 or ML210 (250 nM for NRAS(G12D), 500 nM for 4T1 and D4M.3A, and 1,000 nM for BRAF(V600E) and MC38 cells), doxorubicin (10 µM) or treatment with 150 mJ cm−2 UVB. 8 h later, cancer cells were washed three times with PBS and cultivated for another 16 h in complete RPMI or DMEM. The cell supernatant was collected, centrifuged at 600g for 5 min to remove dead cell debris and stored at −20 °C until further use. All cell lines were routinely tested for mycoplasma contamination in-house by PCR. No further cell line authentications were conducted in the laboratory.

According to recent reports, cancer cell lines were detached by trypsinization (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and washed three times in sterile PBS (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells were injected subcutaneously in 100 μl endotoxin-free PBS on the flank of recipient mice, using 2 × 105 cells for tumour growth studies and 2 × 106 cells for all other experiments. Tumour growth was measured using a digital calliper. Tumour diameters stated in the figures refer to the average values of the longest diameter and its perpendicular for each tumour. Tumour growth was restricted to a maximum diameter of 15 mm, which served as the humane end point and was not exceeded in any of the experiments. For animals reaching the humane end point before the end of the observation period, the last measured tumour diameter was carried forwards to subsequent time points (last observation carried forwards). For experiments involving ferroptotic control or Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E)–OVA melanoma cells, cancer cells were pre-treated with 1 μM RSL3 for 8 h before subcutaneous injection of 1 × 106 cells in 100 μl of endotoxin-free PBS into the flank of recipient mice.

To deplete CD8+ T cells, mice received intraperitoneal injections of 100 µl anti-mouse CD8β antibody (200 µg per mouse; 53-5.8, BioXCell) every 5 days, beginning on day 1 following tumour cell inoculation.

Industry observers note that treatment of mice bearing subcutaneous MC38 or control BRAF(V600E) tumours was initiated once tumours were palpable, on days 3–5 post-tumour cell transplantation. Solutions were prepared fresh every day. For induction of ferroptosis, mice received daily intraperitoneal injection of 40 mg kg−1 IKE dissolved in 55% PEG 300 (Sigma) and 45% PBS. Lyophilized CXB (MedChem) was weighed using a fine balance and made up in a 60:40 ratio of DMSO (1 part, Sigma)/PEG400 (5 parts, Sigma):dH2O. The final concentration was 6 mg ml−1, corresponding to a dose of 30 mg kg−1 delivered in a total volume of 100 µl per mouse. CXB was administered daily by oral gavage.

Tumours, lymph nodes or spleens of tumour cell-inoculated mice were collected at the indicated time points after cancer cell transplantation. Tumour or organ weight was measured using a microscale. For flow cytometry analysis, tumour samples were mechanically dissociated and digested with DNase I (100 µg ml–1, Merck) and collagenase IV (200 U ml–1, Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 40 min at 37 °C followed by filtration through a 70-µm and a 30-µm cell strainer (Miltenyi) and washing with FACS buffer (PBS with 1% FCS and 2 mM EDTA) to generate single-cell suspensions before proceeding with antibody-mediated staining. Spleens were passed through a 70-µm cell strainer, followed by red blood cell lysis with ACK-lysis buffer for 3 min and additional filtration using a 30-µm cell strainer. Lymph nodes were dissociated using a 30-µm cell strainer.

According to recent reports, the following antibodies and staining reagents were used for flow cytometry or cell sorting: fixable viability dye eFluor 450 (dilution: 1:1,000; Thermo Fisher Scientific); fixable viability dye APC-eF780 (1:2,000; Thermo Fisher Scientific); PE-Cy7 anti-CD8α (1:200; 53-6.7, BioLegend); PE-Dazzle594 anti-CD8α (1:200; 53-6.7, BioLegend); BV711 anti-mouse/human-CD44 (1:100; IM7, BioLegend); PerCP-Cy5.5 anti-mouse/human-CD44 (1:100; IM7, BioLegend); PE anti-CD45.1 (1:100; A20, BioLegend); BV510 anti-CD45.2 (1:100; 104, BD Biosciences); BUV395 anti-CD45.2 (1:100; 104, BD Biosciences); FITC anti-CD62L (1:100; MEL-14, BioLegend); FITC anti-CD103 (1:100; M290, BD Biosciences); Pe-Cy7 anti-CD103 (1:100; 2E7; BioLegend); PE-Dazzle594 anti-CD186/CXCR6 (1:200; SA051D1, BioLegend); BV421 anti-CD366/TIM-3 (1:200; RMT3-23, BioLegend); BV605 anti-CD279/PD-1 (1:100; 29F.1A12, BioLegend); PerCP/Cy5.5 anti-TCRβ (1:100; H57-597, BioLegend); AF700 anti-TCRβ (1:100; H57-597, Sony); APC anti-human GZMB (1:200; GB12, Thermo Fisher Scientific); PE anti-human GZMB (1:200; GB12; Thermo Fisher Scientific); FITC anti-Ki-67 (1:100; SolA-15, Thermo Fisher Scientific); PE anti-mouse TCF1 (1:200; S33-966, BD Biosciences); and rabbit-anti-mouse-TCF1/TCF7 (1:100; C.725.7, Thermo Fisher Scientific). This was followed by staining with AF647 donkey-anti-rabbit IgG (1:200; Poly4064, BioLegend); BV605 anti-CD11b (1:200; M1/70; BioLegend); PerCP-Cy5.5 anti-CD11c (1:200; N418; BioLegend); PE-Cy7 anti-CD11c (1:200; M17/4; BioLegend); BV421 anti-XCR1 (1:200; ZET; BioLegend); PE anti-CXCL9 (1:100; MIG-2F5.5, BioLegend); PerCP/Cy5.5 anti-IL-12/IL-23 p40 (1:100; C15.6, BioLegend); FITC anti-I-A/I-E (MHC class II) (1:1,000; M5/114.15.2, Thermo Fisher Scientific); AF700 anti-mouse H-2kb (1:100; AF6-88.5, BioLegend); AF647 anti-CD86 (1:200; GL-1, BioLegend); BV605 anti-CD80 (1:200; 16-10A1, BioLegend); and BV421 anti-CD3 (1:200; 17A2, BioLegend).

Recent findings suggest that staining of the cell surface with fluorescently labelled antibodies and viability dyes was performed for 20 min at 4 °C in FACS buffer (PBS with 1% FCS and 2 mM EDTA). For intracellular staining of GZMB, TCF1 and Ki-67, cells were fixed and permeabilized using the True-Nuclear Transcription Factor Buffer Set (BioLegend) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Intracellular staining of CXCL9 or IL-12 was performed using the Intracellular Fixation & Permeabilization Buffer Set (Thermo Fisher) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Intracellular staining was performed overnight in permeabilization buffer at 4 °C. Flow cytometry analyses were performed using a ID7000C Spectral Cell Analyzer (ID7000 software v2.0.2.17121, Sony Biotechnologies) or a SP6800 Spectral Cell Analyzer (spectral analyser software v2.0.2.14140, Sony Biotechnologies). Flow cytometric quantification of cell numbers was done using CountBright Absolute Counting Beads (Thermo Fisher Scientific). All flow cytometric data were analysed using FlowJo (v10.10.0, BD Biosciences). Sorting of naive OT-I T cells (CD45.1+CD8+CD62L+CD44–) from blood for adoptive transfer experiments and mouse cDC1s (CD103+) from bone marrow cultures was performed using a SH800S Cell Sorter (cell sorter software v2.1.6, Sony Biotechnologies). Representative flow cytometry-gating strategies for analyses of CD8+ TILs, intratumoural cDC1s and cDC2s or splenic cDC1s and cDC2s can be found in Supplementary Fig. 1.

It has been revealed that for adoptive transfer of OVA-specific OT-I cells, 1 × 103 congenically marked naive CD8+ T cells (CD45.1+CD8+CD62L+CD44−) were isolated from the blood of OT-I donor mice and injected intravenously into sex-matched CD45.2+ recipient mice in 100 µl sterile PBS. The transfer was performed 6 h before subcutaneous transplantation of ferroptotic control or Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− BRAF(V600E)–OVA melanoma cells.

Industry observers note that volumetric immunofluorescence tumour microscopy was performed as previously described45. In brief, tumours were fixed in Antigenfix solution (Diapath). Samples were dehydrated in 30% sucrose, embedded in TissueTek OCT freezing medium (Sakura Finetek) and stored at −80 °C. Consecutive sections of 50 μm thickness were generated using a Leica CM3050 S cryostat. Sections were permeabilized, blocked and stained in 0.1 M Tris (Carl Roth) supplemented with 1% BSA, 0.3% Triton X-100 (Merck), normal mouse serum (Merck) and donkey serum (Merck). Stained sections were mounted in Mowiol (Merck) and analysed using an inverted TCS SP8 confocal microscope (Leica), a STELLARIS confocal microscope (Leica) or a THUNDER imager (Leica) for tiled imaging using a HC PL APO CS2 ×20/0.75 NA objective or a HC PL APO CS2 ×40/1.30 NA THUNDER objective, or a Fluoview FV3000 microscope using an UPlanSApo ×20 air/0.75 NA objective (Olympus). All images were acquired as tiled image stacks, covering whole-tumour sections in the xy plane, with 2-μm z-spacing to provide large three-dimensional (3D) image volumes of at least 20 μm depth. Image analysis and cell rendering was performed as previously described45. 3D images were analysed using the Imaris 10.2.0 software (Oxford Instruments). The Imaris surface generation tool was used to reconstruct and visualize 3D objects for individual cells. Clusters of interacting cDC1s and CD8+ T cells were identified in a multi-step process using positional information for cell objects. CD8+ T cell clusters were defined as a minimum of five cells within a distance of 20 μm measured from the outer surface of each cell and identified using the Imaris built-in ‘distance to 5 nearest neighbours’ function. cDC1s interacting with clustered CD8+ T cells (referred to as ‘interacting cDC1’) were identified using object–object closest distance (distance ≤ 5 μm). To identify clustered CD8+ T cells interacting with cDC1s (‘interacting CD8+ T cells’), CD8+ T cells localized more than 15 μm from these interacting cDC1s were removed by distance thresholding using the Imaris filter function. Quantification of cell clusters was performed relative to the volume of the imaged section.

Industry observers note that the following antibodies were used for staining of mouse tissues: AF594 anti-CD3 (1:200; clone 17A2, BioLegend), BV421 anti-CD8α (1:100; clone 53-6.7; BioLegend), anti-CD103 (1:200; goat polyclonal; R&D Systems), FITC anti-MHC class II I-A/I-E (1:500; clone M5/114.15.2, BioLegend), AF680 anti-goat IgG (1:500; donkey polyclonal; Jackson ImmunoResearch), anti-COX2 (1:200; amino acids 584–598; Cayman Chemicals) and AF647 anti-rabbit IgG (1:400; A-21244, Invitrogen). All antibodies were either validated by the manufacturer or were previously reported for immunofluorescence microscopy.

Industry observers note that live-cell imaging was performed using a DMi8 microscope (Leica) with a HC PL APO ×20/0.8 PH2 or HC PL APO ×40/0.95 CORR PH2 objective. Temperature was regulated at 37 °C and CO2 level at 5% using a Heating Unit 2000 (Pecon) equipped with a TempController 2000 (Pecon) and CO2-Controller 2000 (Pecon). Pfa1 cells (2 × 104) were seeded in a µ-slide glass-bottom chamber slide (Ibidi) and cultivated for 24 h before imaging. Dyes for the staining of lipid peroxidation using BODIPY C11 (2 µM; Thermo Fisher Scientific), Ca2+ influx using Fluo-8-AM (4 µM; AAT Bioquest) or CalBryte 630-AM (5 µM; AAT Bioquest), small-molecule influx using FITC-labelled dextrans of 4 kDa or 70 kDa and membrane permeabilization as a marker for cell death using Sytox blue (5 µM; Thermo Fisher Scientific) or 7-AAD (1:40; Thermo Fisher Scientific) were added 30 min before imaging and kept in the media for the time of imaging. To assess lipid peroxidation by BODIPY staining, BODIPY 581/591 C11 (Thermo Fisher) was added directly into the cell culture media at a final concentration of 2 µM and cells were incubated for 30 min at 37 °C before being washed three times with PBS. For live-cell microscopy-based single-cell analyses, BODIPY C11 was kept in the media for the time of imaging. Measurement of oxidized BODIPY C11 was performed after excitation by a 488 nm laser, and measurement of non-oxidized BODIPY C11 after excitation with a 581 nm laser.

Recent findings suggest that for immunohistochemistry, formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded tumour tissue sections were heated at 60 °C for 15 min and deparaffinized with xylene and graded ethanol. Sections were washed in TBS containing 0.01% Tween-20 (TBS-T) and blocked with 5% normal goat serum in TBS-T for 20 min at room temperature. Sections were then incubated overnight at 4 °C with mouse monoclonal anti-4-HNE antibody (1:200; HNEJ-2, JaICA) diluted in TBS-T containing 5% goat serum. After three washes in TBS-T, endogenous peroxidase activity was quenched by incubation with 0.3% H2O2 in methanol for 20 min, followed by three washes in TBS-T. Sections were incubated with biotinylated goat anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody (1:200; 115-065-166, Jackson ImmunoResearch) in TBS-T containing 5% goat serum for 30 min at room temperature, followed by incubation with the VECTASTAIN Elite ABC peroxidase system (PK-6100, Vector Laboratories) for 30 min at room temperature. After washing, sections were visualized using DAB substrate (SK-4100, Vector Laboratories), with development monitored microscopically until a suitable brown colour was obtained. The reaction was stopped by washing with water, and sections were counterstained with haematoxylin, blued in tap water, dehydrated through graded ethanol and xylene, and mounted in Roti Mounting medium (Carl Roth).

Generation of cDC1s was performed as previously described19, with minor modifications. In brief, bone marrow cells were isolated from mouse femur and tibia by flushing the bones with RPMI using a syringe and a 20-gauge cannula. After red blood cell lysis using ACK buffer (double-distilled H2O (ddH2O) with 150 mM ammonium chloride, 10 mM potassium bicarbonate and 1μm disodium EDTA) for 3 min at room temperature, 1.5 × 106 cells per millilitre were incubated with GM-CSF (300 pg ml−1) and FLT3L (55 ng ml−1) in RPMI 1640 medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific) supplemented with 10% FCS (PAN-Biotech), 50 µM β-mercaptoethanol (Thermo Fisher Scientific), 50 U ml–1 penicillin (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and 50 µg ml–1 streptomycin (Thermo Fisher Scientific). After 9 days of culture, non-adherent cells were reseeded at 0.3 × 106 cells per millilitre in fresh medium containing GM-CSF and FLT3L for an additional 5 days before FACS sorting of differentiated cDC1s based on CD103 expression. For assays using splenic cDCs, freshly isolated mouse spleens were digested in RPMI 1640 containing DNase I (100 µg ml–1; Merck) and collagenase IV (200 U ml–1; Thermo Fisher Scientific) for 30 min. Dendritic cells were subsequently isolated using the Pan Dendritic Cell Isolation Kit, mouse (130-100-875, Miltenyi Biotec), according to the manufacturer’s protocol.

For in vitro treatment with cancer cell conditioned medium, mouse cDC1s were cultured with conditioned medium from cancer cells at 37 °C for 16 h before their analysis or use in functional assays. For assessment of cytokine and chemokine production following activation, cDC1s were stimulated with poly(I:C) (10 μg ml−1) for 4 h, and brefeldin A (5 μg ml−1) was added for the last 3 h of stimulation before proceeding with antibody staining for flow cytometric analyses. In some experiments, cDC1 stimulation was done using IFNγ (10 ng ml−1), IFNα (10 ng ml−1), 2′,3′-cGAMP (10 μM), NAD (10 μM) or ATP (100 μM). For the generation of cDC1 conditioned medium, cDC1s were first treated with cancer cell conditioned medium for 16 h, washed three times with PBS and stimulated with poly(I:C) (10 μg ml−1) for 24 h. The culture supernatant was collected and centrifuged at 600g for 5 min to remove remaining cell material, and the cell-free conditioned medium was collected and stored at −20 °C until further use.

To generate antigen-experienced stem-like CD8+ T cells, naive CD8+ T cells were isolated from the spleens of mice using MACS separation and stimulated with mouse anti-CD3/CD28 microbeads and IL-2 (85 U ml–1) for 4 days. After 2 days of culture, CD8+ T cells were re-seeded at 1 × 106 cells per millilitre with fresh medium containing anti-CD3/28 microbeads plus IL-2. To assess the ability of cDC1s to promote antigen-experienced CD8+ T cell expansion, 2.5 × 104 CD8+ T cells from T cell cultures were incubated with mouse anti-CD3/CD28 microbeads in the presence or absence of supernatant from cDC1s pre-treated as indicated in the figure legends. After 72 h of incubation, the number of viable CD3+CD8+ T cells was quantified by flow cytometry.

In a recent development, resazurin (7-hydroxy-10-oxidophenoxazin-10-ium-3-one, sodium; Stemcell) was added directly to the culture medium at a final concentration of 50 µg ml−1 and incubated for 1 h at 37 °C. Viability was measured at an excitation/emission wavelength of 540/590 nm using a Tecan infinite M1000Pro and Tecan i-control software (v3.9.1.0). Cell viability was calculated as the percentage of fluorescence intensity relative to the vehicle control group.

PGE2 concentration in cell-free conditioned medium was measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) (Cayman Chemical) according to the manufacturer’s protocol using a Tecan infinite M1000Pro and Tecan i-control software (v3.9.1.0).

Cytokine and chemokine concentrations in conditioned medium from stimulated cDC1s were quantified using the LEGENDplex bead-based multiplex immunoassay (BioLegend) according to the manufacturer’s protocol.

To block the influx of extracellular Ca2+ into ferroptotic cells, the calcium-chelator EGTA (2 mM) or the osmoprotectant PEG 3350 (10 mM) was added to the cell culture media 4 h after cancer cell treatment with the ferroptosis inducer RSL3.

Cells were lysed in RIPA lysis buffer (150 mM NaCl, 5 mM EDTA, 50 mM Tris, 1% NP-40, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate and 0.1% SDS in ddH20) containing protease and phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (Sigma-Aldrich), sonicated three times for 10 s at 35 kHz and centrifuged at 15,000g at 4 °C for 5 min. The supernatant was collected and used as the protein sample. Western blotting was performed by standard immunoblotting procedure with 12% SDS–PAGE gel and nitrocellulose membrane. Primary antibody staining to GPX4 (1:2,000; EPNCIR144, Abcam), COX2 (1:1,000; amino acids 584–598; Cayman Chemical), β-actin (1:2,000; #4967S, Cell Signaling), p38 (1:1,000; #9212S, Cell Signaling), phospho-p38 (1:1,000; D3F9, Cell Signaling), p38α (1:1,000; #9218S, Cell Signaling) or HSP60 (1:2,000; D6F1, Cell Signaling) was performed at 4 °C overnight. Horseradish peroxidase-labelled secondary antibodies to mouse IgG (1:10,000; RRID: AB_10015289, Jackson ImmunoResearch) or rabbit IgG (1:10,000; RRID: AB_2313567, Jackson ImmunoResearch) were stained for 1 h at room temperature. Bands were visualized using Pierce ECL Western Blotting Substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Images were taken with a ChemiDoc XRS+ (Bio-Rad). Images were analysed with Image Lab software (v6.0.1; Bio-Rad). Images of all uncut blots can be found in Supplementary Fig. 2.

According to recent reports, cell-free conditioned media from cancer cells were mixed 1:1 with methanol (50% v/v) immediately after collection and stored at −80 °C. For analysis, 200 µl of each sample was thawed on ice, spiked with 10 µl of an internal standard mix (final concentration of 5 ng ml−1) and precipitated with 50 µl cold methanol (−20 °C). After protein denaturation on ice (10 min) and centrifugation (10,000g for 15 min at 4 °C), supernatants were adjusted to 1 ml with Milli-Q water. Eicosanoids were extracted using Strata-X 33-µm polymeric reversed-phase SPE plates (Phenomenex) on a Positive Pressure-96 Processor (Waters). Columns were conditioned with methanol and water, and samples were loaded and washed with 10% methanol. Target analytes were eluted in 100% methanol. Eluates were evaporated under nitrogen at 30 °C and reconstituted in 30 µl of 50% methanol. Ten microlitres were injected onto a Sciex QTRAP 6500+ mass spectrometer associated with an Exion UHPLC operated in negative-ion mode using scheduled multiple reaction monitoring. Quantification was carried out using calibration curves and internal standards, with quality control pools and blank samples analysed throughout the run to ensure accuracy and reproducibility. For BRAF(V600E), NRAS(G12D), 4T1 and MC38 cancer cell lines, fold change of each analyte production during ferroptosis relative to DMSO control group was plotted against its final concentration in ferroptotic conditioned medium. For Pfa1 cells, analytes from each oxylipin subclass (eicosanoid, hydroxylated/oxidized lipids and protectins/resolvins) were ordered from high to low abundance in ferroptotic-conditioned medium and plotted as a z-score between different treatment groups.

RNA was isolated using Monarch Total RNA Miniprep kit (New England Biolabs) and complementary DNA (cDNA) was generated using a SensiFAST cDNA synthesis kit (Bioline). Quantitative real-time PCR was performed on a LightCycler 480 (LightCycler 480 software v1.5.1, Roche) using the TAKYON No ROX SYBR MasterMix dTTP Blue kit (Eurogentec) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Gene expression was normalized to the reference gene Hprt by using the ΔCt method. All primers were purchased from Eurofins.

Industry observers note that in vitro-generated WT or ItgaxcrePtger2−/−Ptger4fl/fl CD103+ cDC1s were incubated for 16 h with conditioned medium from control or Ptgs1/Ptgs2−/− ferroptotic BRAF(V600E) melanoma cells followed by stimulation with poly(I:C) (10 μg ml−1) for an additional 4 h. RNA was isolated using an Arcturus PicoPure RNA isolation kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Library preparation was carried out using the Novogene manufactured internal kit. mRNA was purified from total RNA using poly-T oligo-attached magnetic beads. After fragmentation, the first strand cDNA was synthesized using random hexamer primers, followed by the second strand cDNA synthesis using dUTP for directional (strand-specific) library construction. Sequencing was performed on a NovaSeq X Plus with 25B flowcell 2 × 150 bp paired-end sequencing (300 cycles kit). The raw fastq files related to the sequence reads were mapped to the mouse genome, which was downloaded from the UCSC browser (GRCm38/mm10), using the STAR algorithm46. The reads were counted using the Rsubread R package47. These read counts were normalized, and differentially expressed genes were analysed using the iDEP (v2.01) web server48, utilizing the DESeq2 R package49 for differentially expressed gene identification (with fold change ≥ 1.5 and adjusted P < 0.05). Principal component analysis was performed using the prcomp R function and plotted using the ggplot2 R package. Volcano plots were rendered using the Enhanced Volcano R package (https://github.com/kevinblighe/EnhancedVolcano). The ‘Core functional cDC1’ gene set was defined as activation-induced genes significantly downregulated in activated cDC1s following incubation with conditioned medium from ferroptotic control BRAF(V600E) cells. Hierarchical clustering of core functional cDC1 genes was performed using the hclust function in R (Euclidean distance, complete linkage), and heatmaps were generated using the heatmap.2 function of the gplots R package. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was performed on core functional cDC1 genes and arranged according to log2(fold changes). Enrichment of gene sets was then conducted using GSEA (v4.2.3)50. Gene sets related to cytokine signalling and cell migration were extracted from the Molecular Signature Database (https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/msigdb/index.jsp). Gene signatures for antigen uptake and cross-presentation were from a previous study51. The gene set for PGE2 impaired functional cDC1 genes was from a previous study19. PGE2-impaired core functional cDC1 genes for correlation analysis were defined as activation-induced genes significantly downregulated in activated cDC1s following incubation with PGE2. The PreRanked tool from GSEA (v4.2.3) was used to assess the normalized enrichment score, and a false discovery rate (q < 0.25) was utilized to evaluate the statistical significance of the normalized enrichment score.

It has been revealed that throughout this study, different statistical tests were used to assess statistical significance, as indicated in the figure legends. Data are shown as the mean ± s.e.m., mean ± minimum and maximum values or boxplots, as indicated in the figure legends.

Sources indicate that data shown in Figs. 1e and 3g are pooled from two independent experiments. Data shown in Figs. 1b,d, 2b,c,h–k,m–q, 3f,i and 4d,g are representative of two independent experiments. For the boxplots in Figs. 1b, 2h–k,m–o and 3i, the centre line indicates the mean and the bounds show the minimum and maximum values. For the boxplots in Figs. 1e and 4c,e,f,h,i,k, the centre line indicates the median, the bounds extend from the 25th to 75th percentiles and the whiskers correspond to the minimum and maximum values. GraphPad Prism software (v9.5.0 and v9.5.1) was used for statistical analyses.

The pre-built mouse reference genome GRCm38/mm10 was obtained from the UCSC Genome Browser (https://hgdownload.soe.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/mm10/bigZips/). The cytokine signalling gene set was obtained from the Molecular Signatures Database (v2023.1.Mm, Subramanian et al.50; https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/msigdb). The cell migration gene set was custom compiled and obtained from a previous study19. Gene signatures for antigen uptake and cross-presentation were obtained from Kelly and Trowsdale51. The gene set for PGE2-impaired functional cDC1 genes was obtained from Bayerl et al.19. Lists for all gene sets used for GSEA can be found in Supplementary Table 3. #49543. Breaking: Floyd Samba’s Man City debut double has father Chris dancing

Breaking: Floyd Samba’s Man City debut double has father Chris dancing

📅 17 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4094 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There was very much a Samba beat to this Manchester City victory – and it almost had a famous father in the crowd up dancing.
  • This was a night when Brazilian Allan Elias scored his first goal on an enterprising first appearance for City.
  • But it was another debutant who stole the show as the Carabao Cup holders sailed past Norwich City to set up a fourth-round meeting with Brighton.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There was very much a Samba beat to this Manchester City victory – and it almost had a famous father in the crowd up dancing.

This was a night when Brazilian Allan Elias scored his first goal on an enterprising first appearance for City.

But it was another debutant who stole the show as the Carabao Cup holders sailed past Norwich City to set up a fourth-round meeting with Brighton.

Floyd Samba scored two fine goals and had a hand in another on a dream debut that had his beaming dad up off his seat and thrusting his arms in the air as if ready to party.

If the Samba surname feels familiar, that is because Floyd’s father Christopher played more than 200 games for Blackburn Rovers, Queens Park Rangers and Aston Villa.

In fact, it was very much a family affair as Floyd’s brothers Tyrone and Emerson, who are also in City’s academy and hoping one day to tread a similar path, joined in the jubilant celebrations alongside their mother, a visibly emotional Theresa.

It has been revealed that this particular evening belonged to Floyd, though. Deployed as a lone striker by Enzo Maresca, you would not have known he ordinarily plays as a midfielder such was the confidence and composure the 17-year-old oozed.

Norwich could not live with him or City for that matter as Maresca’s impressive start as manager since replacing Pep Guardiola continued apace.

This must have been an incredibly satisfying moment for Samba Sr. He came through incredible hardship – at one stage as a teenager he was rough-sleeping – to forge an impressive career totalling more than 450 games for club and country.

So to be in a position to now have three sons in City’s academy and one produce a debut like this will fill him with enormous pride. Floyd was later seen enjoying a warm embrace with his dad in the crowd, moments after being congratulated by Tyrone, a year his senior, and 12-year-old Emerson, who plays for City’s Under-13s.

According to recent reports, “I knew there would be an opportunity to get some minutes for the first time with the first team – to get a debut like that is mind blowing,” Samba said. “I couldn’t believe it myself, but that’s just the beginning, I’ve got a big career ahead of me. It was a great debut.”.

Floyd caught the eye with a fine free-kick in City’s 2-1 FA Youth Cup final victory over Manchester United last season and now he has goals for the senior side to his name. Pretty stunning they were, too.

The first was a superbly steered header past two Norwich bodies on the line from Allan’s cross and the second a lovely, nonchalantly curled finish low into the far corner.

It has been revealed that what a moment for Floyd Samba! 😍A goal on his Man City debut for the 17-year-old, son of former Blackburn defender Chris 🩵 pic.twitter.com/VCVfX9HCNn.

Sources indicate that chris Samba has deliberately kept a low profile, keen to let his sons get on with their own careers free of distractions, but there was no chance he was going to be able to suppress his emotions in that instant. And nor should he. It was some moment for the boy and his family.

Industry observers note that as impressed as Maresca was by the goals, it will have been other elements of Samba’s game that also caught the eye. He did extremely well to hold off the attentions of Norwich’s centre-backs when receiving a pass from Ayyoub Bouaddi and then returning the ball to the Moroccan who released Rayan Cherki through to score City’s second. His movement was also sharp, at one point taking a difficult pass sweetly in an adjusted strike, only for Norwich’s Bruno Alves to come across to make a timely intervention before Samba could get his shot off.

"Was there any doubt?"Ayyoub Bouaddi with his first assist for Man City as he sets up Rayan Cherki to make it 2-0 🔵 pic.twitter.com/0gfxp5GDXy.

Sources indicate that “It was satisfying not just for the two goals but for the entire performance,” Maresca said. “He didn’t play many games as a nine but he was good. He’s young, full of energy, strong, he can finish.”.

Allan, a £34m summer signing from Palmeiras, will have been just as pleased with his contribution. Maresca’s fluid formation initially resembled a 3-1-5-1 with Allan effectively operating as a right wing-back but he stuck doggedly to the task before eventually getting the moment to showcase his quality, first with his cross for Samba and later with a neat solo run and finish.

Driving inside Sam Field and then cutting back inside the Norwich man before curling an inch perfect finish into the bottom corner – all of it done with his left foot – it was quite the introduction.

According to recent reports, allan on his debut! 🇧🇷Magic from the Brazilian to make it 3-0 to Man City 💥 pic.twitter.com/nw6lNqh1yL.

Hugo Viana, City’s director of football, has mentioned supporters will need to be patient with Allan and that it may take the 22-year-old time to adjust to English football but this first outing will do his confidence plenty of good.

“It was important for him to play 90 minutes and to see a little bit the English competition that is a bit different from South America so overall was good,” Maresca said.

According to recent reports, cherki was the only survivor from the team that started Sunday’s victory over Manchester United but it all felt pretty seamless from City. Bouaddi, the £85m signing from Lille, was poised and graceful in midfield alongside the impressive Mateo Kovacic and Geronimo Rulli could not have asked for a much quieter debut in goal.

FLOYD SAMBA again!! 🌟The 17-year-old curls one in to score his second on his Man City debut with his dad Christopher watching on in the stands 👏 pic.twitter.com/fJ5mfEWBx1.

Nico O’Reilly looked like he had barely broken a sweat despite Norwich’s players routinely being unable to keep up with him. Norwich themselves made nine changes but the gulf in class was enormous and testament to City’s strength in depth.

The game also gave Maresca the opportunity to give run outs to two more academy graduates who played in that Youth Cup final triumph, Kaden Braithwaite and Ryan McAidoo and the latter got his own name on the scoresheet to make it 5-0.

In a recent development, all told there were seven City academy graduates on the pitch, two of them playing for Norwich. This was certainly a night to remember for the club’s youth production line.

It has been revealed that with the dominant performance, Man City have earned themselves the privilege of hosting Brighton in the next round, who will no doubt prove a much stiffer challenge than Norwich. They become the sixth all-Premier League tie in the next round, with only Fleetwood, Bradford and Peterborough remaining from outside the top flight:.

Possession: Man City 66% vs 34% Norwich.

Touches inside opposition box: 30 vs 4.

Erling Haaland left out of the squad, watching from the stands, would have enjoyed that performance from Floyd Samba. Here is his second goal for you to enjoy on his debut night:.

Recent findings suggest that FLOYD SAMBA again!! 🌟The 17-year-old curls one in to score his second on his Man City debut with his dad Christopher watching on in the stands 👏 pic.twitter.com/fJ5mfEWBx1.

Five unanswered goals and a home-grown hero emerges for Manchester City!

Great through ball from O’Reilly, which Lewis lets run past him for the dummy. McAidoo runs on to it on the right of the box and first-time fires it low into the far corner.

It has been a perfect night for Manchester City’s academy.

According to recent reports, well we look like we’re heading for a matching scoreline to the previous edition of the fixture. That pesky shot on target is still eluding Norwich, whereas Samba is still out there looking for his hat-trick.

Two minutes of time to be added – who will get there first?

O’Reilly sends a high, looping ball to the back post from the left side, where McAidoo rushes to meet it but can’t get over it under pressure.

Final change for Norwich, as Kvistgaarden who has not had much service tonight, comes off for Schwartau.

Bouaddi sends a looping ball across the field to McAidoo, which he picks up on the edge of the box, but he is unable to get the ball under control to take his shot and it is cleared away as far as another City shirt.

The corner comes in to the centre of the box but is headed out by a City shirt.

It’s all slightly too little too late for Norwich.

They get another corner as Musaba tries to send a cross into the box from the right and it is blocked out.

Industry observers note that A free-kick for Norwich now as O’Reilly commits the foul 35 yards out. It goes in towards McConville at the back post, but Ait-Nouri heads it out for a Norwich corner.

Recent findings suggest that mo Touré strays just offside on the edge of the box, as Musaba sends a lovely little ball over to find him on the turn and the forward slots it past Rulli. Celebrations don’t quite begin before the flag goes up but that is a shame for the visitors.

Norwich have managed to get more of a grip in this half, despite conceding two more goals, but they are still without a shot on goal as we approach the final 15 minutes.

Another round of changes for both sides.

Man City take off scorer of their third goal Allan to bring on Braithwaite.

Norwich replace Ben Slimane and Bruno Alves with Touré and McConville.

Samba again at the heart of the action, laying off the ball to McAidoo on the right for the winger to run into the box. His shot towards the far post is saved low by Grimshaw who spills it almost into the path of Lewis, but Norwich survive.

Recent findings suggest that lewis makes a run down the right-hand side and crosses into Samba on the edge of the box. He lays off to McAidoo, but his shot goes sailing over the bar.

A surprise to no one, it is chucking it down in Manchester.

According to recent reports, big cheers from the away end as Norwich get their first corner of the evening. It is lofted high and long to the back post, where it is headed away by Bouaddi. It bounces out to Musaba, who has just come on, and he strikes it from the top of the box on the half-volley.

Sources indicate that his shot cuts through a crowd in the box and has Rulli diving to his left, but it goes wide of the post. What an introduction that would have been!

Well all the stories from this match will be all about young Floyd Samba. Feel free to leave your best punny Samba/dance-related headlines in the comments section.

For Man City as you would expect it is all about game management from here on out.

Some more changes to report for Norwich as well, as Crnac is replaced by Musaba.

Wright is able to run in to space towards the edge of the box, but as has been their story all evening, his pass out to the wing is just not where it needs to be and their effort just breaks down.

What a way to score a second! A night to remember for Floyd Samba!

Industry observers note that norwich try and play out from the back but far too sloppy and Ait-Nouri picks up the ball on the left of the box. He has plenty of time to tee up Samba inside the box at the left corner, who finds himself with plenty of space to curl his shot into the far corner, beating the diving Grimshaw.

We may be seeing plenty more of him this season.

According to recent reports, norwich looking for their way back into the game, as the ball comes down the left, fizzed in low and flashes past Rulli, trying to claim it. It deflects off a crowd of bodies and spins up, but Fisher can’t connect and it spins away harmlessly wide of the goal.

It is definitely Norwich’s best chance of the game and Fisher will be upset he hasn’t made more of that.

According to recent reports, and Allan makes it three! Minutes after the restart, the Brazilian makes his own mark on his debut.

Maresca switched him onto the left side to escape Yongwa, and he picks up the ball outside the box and makes the run inside. He runs circles around Field and slots the ball home into the far bottom corner.

Industry observers note that some changes from both sides at half-time. McAidoo comes on for Cherki, though O’Reilly is the one to move up into midfield to fill the gap.

Norwich take off Diallo for Maghoma.

45 minutes left for the visitors to create something special!

What a moment for Floyd Samba! 😍A goal on his Man City debut for the 17-year-old, son of former Blackburn defender Chris 🩵 pic.twitter.com/VCVfX9HCNn.

Manchester City will be the ones to host Brighton in the next round – giving the visitors the opportunity to pull off a remarkable feat of knocking out both Manchester sides should they win.

Enjoy the highlights from last night as they came from behind to dispatch Man Utd:.

Possession: Man City 72% vs 28% Norwich.

Touches inside opposition box: 15 vs 1.

Industry observers note that and without much ado at the end of the half, we have reached the break. City put themselves in control with two quick-fire goals and it looks a tall task for Norwich to find their way back into the match.

Credit where it is due, Yongwa has been very good for Norwich. He has stood fast, made some very good challenges and stopped Allan getting much of a look-in on the right.

In a recent development, as we approach half-time, the stats tell a sorry story. Norwich have had just 28% possession and created a single shot, none on target.

As City come again, Norwich have pulled every man back to try and keep the situation salvageable before the break.

Samba was in again there, making a run into the box with a ball from Cherki, wrestling with Bruno Alves as he goes. The defender does enough to throw him off and Grimshaw is able to come out and snatch the ball.

Man City are looking to close this out now, and they look threatening every time they break.

Ait-Nouri is the latest to try his luck, making a run into the box from the left, but his shot is blocked.

A few minutes to remember here for Floyd Samba. First he steers home a very well taken header to give City the lead and then he plays a crucial role in the second, holding the ball up well before laying it off to Bouaddi to release Cherki to score. That’s how to make an impression on your debut.

Recent findings suggest that and the floodgates have opened. Two goals in two minutes for the defending champions.

Industry observers note that samba finds Bouaddi in midfield, who takes it forward and feeds Cherki running to his left. He gets himself one-on-one and slots cool as you like into the bottom left corner.

City are in control all of a sudden and Norwich will be devastated.

As soon as I say that, Floyd Samba finds a way through.

Sources indicate that he has looked the brightest for City, and O’Reilly sends a cross over the box from the left, drawing Grimshaw away from position. The ball is pinged back in by Allan and the youngster stoops to meet it, heading in to the bottom corner.

Norwich have been very disciplined in defence so far. Yongwa has been closing down Allan on the wing very well.

Cherki is starting to get some momentum – but is swarmed by yellow shirts as he picks up the ball on the edge of the area.

Another loose ball from City in midfield and Norwich pick it up again. The ball to set the front line free is equally as loose from the visitors though and it breaks down once again.

Sources indicate that samba is looking lively, racing to get on a ball in front of Darling just on the edge of the box. Darling recovers to send it out for a corner, which becomes a free kick after Ait-Nouri wrestles his man to the ground at the back post as City are taking.

Wright sends a long ball across the field, looking for a man on the right side but Rulli is alert to it and comes to claim at the edge of the box.

Kovacic demonstrates some promise with a strong run on the ball down the centre of the field, taking the ball all the way to the edge of the box, where he collides with a defender, and the ball spins away for Norwich to clear out.

This is better from City, who have looked like they’re lacking drive so far.

Yongwa again probing down the left side. It takes two to dispossess him and Man City manage to get the throw in, but approaching 20 minutes Norwich will be happy with this.

Kovacic loses the ball in midfield and Norwich surge forward. The move breaks down as Wright’s pass to Diallo on the wing is just behind him and he can’t take it forward into the box.

Spent the first 10 minutes trying to work out City’s system and settled on a 3-1-5-1, with Bouaddi operating as a nominal third centre-back, but it seems to have changed again now with O’Reilly dropping to left back and Bouaddi stepping into midfield. No doubt the metamorphosis will continue.

This Man City team have never played all together and it is clear that they’re still settling in here, figuring out how they’re going to press here.

Kovacic in the captain’s armband is tying it all together in midfield.

Khusanov threads a lovely ball to Samba who flicks it into the path of Lewis, who takes it and makes a run into the box. He creates space and sends a right-footed shot over the bar – but Man City are building.

Sources indicate that norwich make a move forward, with Yongwa bringing the ball down the left side but his cross into the box is blocked by Allan sliding in. The Brazilian is then fouled again as Yongwa tries to reclaim the ball and Man City get back in possession.

Industry observers note that it’s actually three Samba brothers at City. The youngest, Emerson, is also in the academy.

Early foul on Allan gets Man City a free kick and they have started as everyone expected they would – in plenty of possession.

They look for the early goal as O’Reilly feeds him in the from the left side, but the shot is blocked.

We have kicked off in Manchester!

With just over 10 minutes until kick-off here are the teams for tonight’s fixture:.

It’s nine changes for Norwich from the squad that lost 4-3 to Middlesbrough on the weekend.

Norwich goalkeeper Daniel Grimshaw came through the ranks at Manchester City, joining as a teenager, so this will be a special night for the 28-year-old.

Speaking of Phil Foden, the winger will not be making an appearance tonight, as he is serving his three-match suspension following his sending off in the Manchester derby. The England international lashed out at Bruno Fernandes after the United captain had fouled him, resulting in a red card for violent conduct.

As well as this fixture, he will also be missing City’s game against Sunderland and the trip to Anfield to face Liverpool the following weekend.

We broke down the incident as it happened on Sunday and you can get the full story here.

Heavy squad rotation (10 changes in total for Maresca) has handed debuts for Gero Rulli in goal, as well as Allan and Floyd Samba in the outfield.

A versatile midfielder, he has totalled 24 appearances across six competitions (incl Premier League 2) and scored 17 and assisted six goals in those matches.

Keep your eyes on young midfielder Floyd Samba, who has been handed his Manchester City debut tonight against Norwich by manager Enzo Maresca. Floyd is the 17 year old son of former Blackburn Rovers defender Christopher Samba.

His older brother Tyrone, 18, also plays for City. The siblings played in City’s FA Youth Cup final win over Manchester United last season, with Floyd scoring the first in a 2-1 win.

City fans will also be keen to see how Allan Elias gets on on his first start, having arrived from Palmeiras for £34m. Geronimo Rulli also debuts in goal.

Sources indicate that these two sides have not met since 2022, when Norwich were still in the top flight and were beaten 4-0 by City. Looking at their previous meetings, the odds are definitely stacked in favour of Enzo Maresca’s side, who have scored 14 unanswered goals in their last three meetings with Norwich, while the Championship side have not scored any.

City will be looking to make it six straight wins across all competitions tonight, having started perfectly in the Premier League with four wins from four, and comfortably seeing off Porto in their Champions League opener.

They were the talk of the weekend with their deeply controversial 1-0 win over rivals Manchester United as – having gone down to 10 men after Phil Foden was sent off – their winning goal was allowed to stand despite Enzo Fernández being clearly in an offside position that impacted United’s keeper and backline.

Recent findings suggest that philippe Clement’s side beat MK Dons 4-1 in the first round, and followed that up with a 2-1 win over Cardiff City in the second to reach the Etihad tonight. The fourth-round draw has already been done, and it has been decided that the winner of this match will face Brighton.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Sam Varley | 19 Nov 2026 23:57.

Aiming to build a lead at the top of the League One table on the return from the international break, Huddersfield Town will welcome Leicester City to the Accu Stadium on Saturday.

The hosts currently lead second-placed Stockport County on goal difference while their visitors sit 11th and four points off the top six.

Huddersfield Town return from the November international break on Saturday aiming to pick up where they left off and pull clear at the top of the League One table.

Aiming to kick on from two disappointing years in England's third tier and fight for promotion back to the Championship, following the permanent appointment of Martin Drury over the summer, they have enjoyed an impressive campaign thus far, right now sitting top having earned 29 points from their first 14 games, winning eight and only losing one of those.

That solitary defeat came in mid-September, and the Terriers have won five and drawn two of seven league outings since, having taken on Luton Town in their final game before the break on the back of four straight victories over Plymouth Argyle, Peterborough United, Wigan Athletic and Bradford City, scoring 11 goals and conceding just two across those.

Drury's men had to settle for a point, though, levelling early in the second half through Joe Taylor in a 1-1 draw before heading into a pair of cup games, firstly bowing out of the FA Cup to fourth-tier Exeter City.

They would then beat Liverpool Under-21s 4-0 in the EFL Trophy last weekend, and now with their full focus back on League One, presently ahead of Stockport County on goal difference and third-placed Oxford United by three points, Huddersfield Town will hope to continue their hot streak and put another victory on the board.

Their visitors, meanwhile, return from the break with their sights set on the playoff places and the hopes of continuing an improved run of their own.

After suffering back-to-back defeats from the Premier League to League One, and turning to Russell Martin in the summer, Leicester City endured another poor start, managing just two wins and nine in their first eight games.

The Foxes appear to have turned a corner since, though, putting three more wins and a draw on the board in their last five league outings to climb into the top half, having beaten Doncaster Rovers, Bromley and Wigan Athletic alongside an away loss to Luton Town.

Martin's men then hosted Stevenage in their final league game before the break and had to settle for a point, having twice led through Sammy Braybrooke and Kamari Doyle and been pegged back, before they recorded consecutive cup victories, getting the better of Oxford City in the FA Cup and Walsall in the EFL Trophy.

Now also focused back on their League One bid, having moved within four points of the playoff spots and five of fourth place, Leicester City will hope to get back to winning ways with the scalp of the league leaders to move closer to the frontrunners on Saturday.

Huddersfield Town League One form:.

Huddersfield Town form (all competitions):.

Leicester City League One form:.

Leicester City form (all competitions):.

Huddersfield Town will remain without injured defenders Jack Whatmough and Murray Wallace and midfielders Marcus McGuane and Herbie Kane.

Drury fielded a strong team for their EFL Trophy game last week, with star forward Joe Taylor scoring another two goals to go alongside his 10 for the season in League One, and he will continue to spearhead the attack.

Derensili Sanches Fernandes will return to join him after international duty with Cape Verde, having also shone this season with seven goals and six assists in 14 League One appearances.

Leicester City have a relatively clean bill of health, other than long-term injuries for goalkeeper Jakub Stolarczyk and defender Ben Nelson.

Martin found a somewhat settle starting XI for the most part before the break, and Warren O'Hora, Harry Souttar and Caleb Okoli are bound to continue in a back three with Will Alves and Luke Thomas operating as full-backs.

Will Smallbone, John Lundstram and 18-year-old prospect Louis Page are likely left to compete for two midfield spots, while Sammy Braybrooke and Kamari Doyle may again support front man Emil Riis, who has scored six goals in nine league games so far this term, despite competition from Liam Cullen, Wes Burns and Conor Chaplin.

Huddersfield Town possible starting lineup:.

Young; Balker, Bowat, Roughan; Bronkhorst, Humphreys, Collins, Mumba; Sanches Fernandes, Taylor, Fletcher.

Leicester City possible starting lineup:.

McCarthy; O'Hora, Souttar, Okoli; Alves, Lundstram, Page, Thomas; Braybrooke, Riis, Doyle.

Leicester City certainly appear to be improving and showing their class more after a tough start, but they face a tough test away at a formidable Huddersfield Town team who also boast an abundance of quality and have settled into life under Drury perfectly.

With Taylor and Sanches Fernandes both in hot streaks, we fancy the Terriers to come out on top at home in a high-quality encounter.

West Ham United manager Scott Parker has spoken positively about Joël Piroe ahead of Saturday’s Championship clash with Preston North End, raising an interesting question over his starting striker.

During his pre-match press conference, Parker acknowledged the Dutchman’s impressive goalscoring record and revealed that he was looking forward to spending more time working with him.

“I’ve known about Joël, having played against his teams. His goalscoring record is really good,” remarked Parker.

“It’s a shame for us he’s been away, but he’s in good form, and I’m looking forward to working with him more.”.

Personally, I would 100% start Piroe ahead of Taty Castellanos, irrespective of how well the Argentine might have trained during the international break.

Piroe is a proven Championship goalscorer, and Parker knows all about him from his previous experience managing in this division.

I think he very much deserves a run of games in an attempt to fire at least one of our strikers into action.

The alternative is to continue persevering with Castellanos, who has been a considerable disappointment since West Ham’s relegation.

And there is another factor to consider.

As Claret & Hugh exclusively revealed, the club are exploring the possibility of selling Castellanos in January, with Nils Koppen already investigating potential replacements.

Further reports from Argentina have suggested the striker wants to leave, although no departure has been agreed.

Piroe is admired by Scott Parker.

I don’t think there’s any mystery surrounding what Piroe offers.

He knows the Championship, he knows how to score goals in it, and he’s already demonstrated that he can contribute to this West Ham team.

As we’ve previously argued when discussing Parker’s selection options, Piroe has a compelling case to start ahead of Castellanos.

Of course, the manager will have his own ideas about how he wants his centre-forward to play.

But given the lack of goals from our recognised strikers, I’d rather see Parker give the Dutchman a proper opportunity than continue waiting for Castellanos to discover some form.

For me, Piroe starts against Preston.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 08:03 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 09:49 EST, 16 November 2026.
  • Romelu Lukaku has unveiled his retirement from international football in a 'bombshell' decision that has left the Belgian press utterly stunned.
  • The former Chelsea and Manchester United forward, 33, vowed in January that the 2026 World Cup would not be his last major tournament with the Belgium national team, although he now appears to have changed his mind over his future.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By BEN WILLCOCKS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR.

Published: 08:03 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 09:49 EST, 16 November 2026.

Romelu Lukaku has unveiled his retirement from international football in a 'bombshell' decision that has left the Belgian press utterly stunned.

The former Chelsea and Manchester United forward, 33, vowed in January that the 2026 World Cup would not be his last major tournament with the Belgium national team, although he now appears to have changed his mind over his future.

Describing his international career as a 'great ride', Lukaku took to social media on Monday morning to break the unexpected news.

'16 years old,' his Instagram statement began. 'For 16 years, I gave everything for the national team. I experienced every possible emotion. I played with fantastic teammates for whom I will always be grateful.

According to recent reports, 'I want to thank them all. I also want to thank all the coaches for pushing me and giving me the confidence to help the team. It was a great ride, and I enjoyed every moment.

Sources indicate that 'To the Belgian fans, thank you for the support you have given our team. I am proud to have represented my country at four World Cups and three European Championships. I will never forget those moments. I am at peace with my decision to stop here. It was amazing, it was a joy. I am grateful. Thank you.'.

Belgium legend Romelu Lukaku has announced his decision to retire from international football.

Lukaku vowed in January that the 2026 World Cup would not be his last major tournament.

The Belgian forward has fallen down the pecking order and spent a lot of time on the bench.

The Belgian veteran accompanied his post with a gallery of photographs from his storied international career, from his debut against Croatia under Dick Advocaat in 2010 to his final chapter wearing the armband.

Lukaku has captained Belgium on a handful of occasions since 2020, alongside the likes of Kevin De Bruyne and Youri Tielemans.

The 33-year-old forward, who became one of the hottest properties in world football after breaking on the scene at Chelsea, has been a regular fixture in the international set-up for almost two decades.

Spearheading Belgium's golden generation, which included star-studded talents such as De Bruyne, Thibaut Courtois and Eden Hazard, Lukaku chalked up an impressive 135 caps for the international team.

He also retires as Belgium's all-time top scorer on 94 goals, just six shy of a century.

Belgian newspapers were caught out by the shock announcement, which was described as an 'unexpected bombshell' by outlet HLN on Monday.

Lukaku's stock within the international set-up has fallen since he promised the 2026 World Cup would not be his last major tournament in January.

After suffering multiple injury setbacks, he featured at the tournament under Rudi Garcia and continued to play a crucial role, scoring three times as a substitute to guide Belgium to the quarter-finals where they were ultimately stopped by eventual champions Spain.

Since Mark van Bommel's appointment in August, following Garcia's departure at the end of his contract, Lukaku has slipped further down the pecking order, with Charles De Ketelaere preferred to lead the line.

Lukaku, pictured with Kevin De Bruyne, was an unused substitute as Belgium beat Italy 4-1.

Axel Witsel sent a heartfelt message to Lukaku on Instagram: 'Thanks for everything, legend'.

During Belgium's resounding 4-1 victory over Italy on Sunday, Lukaku warmed the bench as an unused substitute - and wasn't even in the squad to face Turkey three days before.

While Belgium were winning in the second half against the Italians, Lukaku was seen warming up on the sidelines in the hope of featuring for one last time, but unfortunately was not given the opportunity.

VTM NIEUWS anchor Maarten Breckx claimed De Bruyne looked 'concerned' while speaking to Lukaku on the bench, suggesting the former Man City star was unhappy to see his team-mate overlooked.

'When it became clear that he wouldn't be allowed to come on, De Bruyne was talking to him. You could see the concern in his eyes,' he said.

Industry observers note that 'You could tell, especially from Romelu's attitude, that he was dissatisfied and displeased. He had probably counted on getting some minutes...'.

While neither are likely to be starters in a team that wins trophies at Old Trafford, the poor physical base of the current squad must be raised, and the duo would elevate the current squad's level.

However, signing those two players would not address wider imbalances in the team given there are serious concerns about the likes of Lisandro Martinez and Bruno Fernandes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mark Noble has provided an interesting insight into how West Ham United’s recruitment operation is working under Scott Parker, revealing that Nils Koppen is in regular contact with the coaching staff about the players the club needs.

Speaking in an interview with West Ham’s official website, Noble explained that the Director of Player Recruitment is arriving at Rush Green as early as 6.30am, watching training and discussing the squad with Parker and his coaches.

It has been revealed that with the January transfer window approaching and West Ham desperate to secure promotion, it’s encouraging to hear that recruitment discussions are taking place. But for me, the most important part of Noble’s revelation has very little to do with what time Koppen arrives for work.

Quite frankly, whether Koppen arrives at half six in the morning is neither here nor there.

Much of the analytical and recruitment work can be carried out perfectly well from wherever somebody can plug into the internet.

What I find far more vital is the open dialogue Noble has described.

He explained that Koppen watches training and that the coaching staff speak openly with him about the players they believe West Ham need.

Koppen then works with the club’s scouts and analysts in the background, allowing Parker and Noble to concentrate on coaching.

That strikes me as a huge plus and potentially a massive step in the right direction.

It also appears to represent a departure from the way things have operated previously, when questions were regularly raised about whether recruitment decisions matched the manager’s requirements.

As we discussed following Parker’s talkSPORT interview, the manager is absolutely right to concentrate on improving the players already at his disposal rather than becoming consumed by January transfers.

But that only works if the recruitment department understands precisely what he needs.

We know from our recent dialogue with a club insider that Koppen has begun looking for another striker, and Noble’s comments suggest those discussions are taking place alongside the coaching staff’s assessment of the squad.

That’s exactly how it should work.

Ultimately, I’m far more interested in whether Koppen signs the right players than whether he’s the first person through the door at Rush Green.

But if the people coaching the team and those recruiting for it are finally speaking openly about what West Ham need, that has to be encouraging.

By Anthony Nolan | 20 Nov 2026 01:15, Last updated: 20 Nov 2026 04:58.

Keen to resume their unlikely Bundesliga title challenge, Freiburg will travel to face promoted side Elversberg at Waldstadion Kaiserlinde on Saturday.

The Black and White are desperate to avoid another defeat, though Die Breisgau-Brasilianer are eyeing their fifth victory on the bounce.

Vincent Wagner's Elversberg have enjoyed an excellent beginning to their Bundesliga campaign, and have performed the best of any of the three promoted clubs this term.

Currently seventh with 13 points, the Black and White are just two points shy of sixth-placed Werder Bremen, and have fifth-placed Bayer Leverkusen within their reach this weekend.

However, Wagner's side signed off for the international break with a 2-1 loss to Borussia Dortmund at Signal Iduna Park, where they were only able to muster a late consolation via Noel Futkeu.

That defeat was to be expected on paper given the level of opposition, but the concerning factor is that it was Elversberg's third beating in four games, with the team avoiding disappointment once in a 4-1 triumph over Mainz 05 on October 30.

To make matters worse, Saturday's hosts have conceded 18 goals in nine games - a rate of two per match - the worst total in the top half of the Bundesliga.

Meanwhile, Julian Schuster's Freiburg will be vying to maintain their high-flying start to the season despite the international break disrupting their form.

Die Breisgau-Brasilianer secured a 2-0 victory over Union Berlin last time out in the league, courtesy of a second-half own goal from Rani Khedira and a follow up from Yuito Suzuki 12 minutes later.

That triumph marked a fourth in a row across all competitions for Schuster's men, who proved that their blip of three consecutive defeats in mid-October was merely a temporary stumble.

Now third with 19 points to their name, Freiburg are sitting just two points behind leaders Bayern Munich and Dortmund, and three clear of fifth-placed Leverkusen.

Though a title race is not out of the question, Champions League qualification alone would represent a major feat for Die Breisgau-Brasilianer.

With the aim of keeping ahead of their European rivals as a minimum, fans of the visitors will draw confidence from the team's attacking prowess, which has seen them score 20 goals so far - an output that has only been bettered by Bayern and RB Leipzig this season.

Elversberg form (all competitions):.

Freiburg form (all competitions):.

Elversberg will be without a number of defenders, including left-back Nicholas Mickelson, who is dealing with a medial collateral ligament injury, as well as centre-backs Lukas Pinckert and Luis Seifert, both of whom have ankle problems.

In their absence, Maximilian Rohr and Florian Le Joncour should start at the heart of Wagner's backline, flanked by Luca Sirch and Lasse Gunther.

As for Freiburg, they are missing left-back Berkay Yilmaz, who is suspended after being sent off for Freiburg II against FC-Astoria Walldorf.

That being said, Jordy Makengo remains available to start on the left of a four-man defence alongside Philipp Lienhart, Matthias Ginter and Philipp Treu.

Further forward, Igor Matanovic is likely to lead the line on Saturday, supported by a trio of Jan-Niklas Beste, Yuito Suzuki and Derry Scherhant.

Kristof; Sirch, Rohr, Le Joncour, Gunther; Poreba, Keidel; Petkov, Onyeka, Krattenmacher; Mokwa.

Freiburg possible starting lineup:.

Backhaus; Treu, Ginter, Lienhart, Makengo; Engelhardt, Eggestein; Beste, Suzuki, Scherhant; Matanovic.

Elversberg may be lingering just outside the top six, but their defensive record suggests that they could be caught out on Saturday.

With that defensive frailty in mind, Freiburg - as one of the most potent attacking sides in the Bundesliga - will be optimistic about their chances against a team that have lost three of their last four matches.
